rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Diesel generator sets are widely used in communication base stations, emergency power supply, engineering equipment, field operations, and other scenarios. In low-temperature environments, diesel viscosity increases, engine oil fluidity decreases, and battery performance declines, which may lead to difficulties in starting the diesel engine. Therefore, preheating before startup is of great significance. At present, some preheating control systems still rely on manual operation, which may cause inaccurate preheating time, unclear status indication, and strong dependence on operators. To improve the reliability of low-temperature startup, this project aims to design an automatic preheating controller based on a domestic microcontroller, realizing functions such as ambient temperature detection, threshold judgment, relay control, status indication, and timeout alarm.

2. Main Tasks

(1) Complete the overall scheme design of the preheating controller: Analyze the low-temperature preheating requirements of diesel generator sets, and determine the system composition, control process, and main technical indicators.

(2) Complete the hardware circuit design: With a domestic microcontroller as the core, design circuits for power supply, temperature detection, key setting, relay driving, and buzzer alarm, meeting the DC18 V–36 V input requirement and basic protection requirements.

(3) Complete the software control program design: Develop the microcontroller control program to realize temperature acquisition, threshold judgment, parameter setting, timing control, relay control, and alarm indication.

(4) Realize the automatic preheating control logic: When the ambient temperature is lower than the set value, the system automatically completes three stages: 120 s preheating, 60 s stop reminder, and automatic stop alarm. The timing error should be controlled within ±0.5 s.

(5) Complete prototype fabrication and test analysis: Fabricate a preheating controller prototype, and test temperature detection, preheating startup, relay operation, indicator flashing, buzzer alarm, and power supply adaptability to verify whether the system meets the design requirements.

3. Expected Outcomes

(1) Complete the requirement analysis and overall design scheme for the diesel generator set preheating control system.

(2) Complete the hardware circuit design and software control program design based on a domestic microcontroller.

(3) Develop a preheating controller experimental prototype and complete basic functional debugging.

(4) Conduct tests on temperature detection, timing accuracy, relay operation, and alarm logic, and form a test result analysis.

(5) Complete the undergraduate graduation thesis, summarizing the design process, test results, and possible improvements.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Histopathology images are produced by examining thin, stained tissue sections under a microscope. They provide important visual information about tissue structure and are commonly used by pathologists when assessing brain tumours. However, pathology images are usually very large and may contain considerable variation in colour, texture, tissue arrangement, and image quality. Reviewing many images manually can therefore be time-consuming.


Deep learning can assist with the preliminary screening and organisation of pathology images. Instead of training a large neural network from the beginning, transfer learning reuses a model that has already learned useful visual features from a large image dataset. The model can then be adapted to a smaller medical-image dataset with relatively limited computing resources.


This project will investigate a simple transfer-learning approach for distinguishing between broad categories of brain histopathology images, such as tumour-related and non-tumour tissue images, or between two selected tumour groups depending on the available dataset. The purpose is not to build a clinical diagnostic system. The emphasis will be on understanding the workflow, preparing image data correctly, training an existing model, and interpreting the results.


2. Main Tasks

  1. Study the basic principles of histopathology imaging, image classification, convolutional neural networks, and transfer learning.
  2. Select a suitable public or supervisor-provided brain histopathology image dataset.
  3. Inspect, organise, resize, and label the images, and divide them into training, validation, and testing groups.
  4. Apply simple image preprocessing and augmentation methods, such as rotation, flipping, cropping, or brightness adjustment.
  5. Adapt one or two pre-trained models, such as ResNet18, MobileNet, or EfficientNet-B0, to the selected classification task.
  6. Train the models using a standard Python deep-learning framework.
  7. Compare the models using accessible evaluation methods, including accuracy, confusion matrices, sensitivity, specificity, and example predictions.
  8. Visualise several correctly and incorrectly classified images and discuss possible reasons for the model’s decisions.

3. Expected Outcomes

The student is expected to produce:

  • a clearly organised brain histopathology image-processing workflow;
  • a working transfer-learning model for a simple two-class or small multi-class classification task;
  • a comparison of one or two lightweight pre-trained neural networks;
  • training and validation curves, confusion matrices, and example classification results;
  • a brief analysis of common errors, dataset limitations, and possible improvements;
  • well-commented Python code with instructions for running the experiments;
  • a final-year dissertation describing the background, methodology, results, limitations, and conclusions.
rows.themeTitle: Transfer Learning-Based Screening of Brain Histopathology Images

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Portable and low-field MRI systems are attracting increasing attention because they are smaller, less expensive, and easier to install than conventional hospital MRI systems. They may therefore be useful in community hospitals, emergency settings, mobile clinics, and regions with limited medical resources.

However, images acquired using portable MRI systems may have lower spatial resolution and less visible anatomical detail than images from conventional MRI systems. This can make small structures and tissue boundaries more difficult to observe.

Deep learning-based image enhancement provides a possible solution. A neural network can learn the relationship between lower-resolution and higher-resolution images and then generate clearer images from lower-quality inputs. Such a method may improve the visual quality of portable MRI images without changing the imaging hardware.

This project will investigate a simple and practical deep learning approach for enhancing the resolution and clarity of portable MRI images.


2. Main Tasks

The student will complete the following main tasks:

  1. Understand the basic problem Learn the basic concepts of MRI image resolution, image quality, and deep learning-based image enhancement. Only introductory knowledge of MRI physics is required.
  2. Prepare an image dataset Use publicly available MRI images or an existing research dataset. Lower-resolution images can be generated from clearer images through controlled downsampling and image degradation.
  3. Build a baseline enhancement model Implement or adapt a simple existing neural network for image enhancement. The project may begin with a basic convolutional neural network or a lightweight super-resolution model.
  4. Train and test the model Train the model to recover clearer images from lower-resolution inputs. The student will learn the standard workflow of data preparation, training, validation, and testing.
  5. Explore simple improvements Investigate manageable improvements such as:
  • different image resizing methods;
  • alternative loss functions;
  • basic data augmentation;
  • different numbers of network layers; or
  • transfer learning from an existing model.
  1. Evaluate the results Compare the enhanced images with the original lower-resolution images using visual assessment and common image-quality indicators such as PSNR and SSIM. Particular attention should be given to whether tissue boundaries and important anatomical details are preserved.

Expected Outcomes

The student is expected to develop a working deep learning pipeline that can enhance the resolution and visual clarity of portable or low-field MRI images. The developed model should aim to produce images that are clearer than the original low-resolution inputs while avoiding excessive smoothing, artificial structures, or loss of important anatomical information.

The final project should include:

  • an organized MRI image dataset or data-processing procedure;
  • working and readable Python code;
  • a trained image-enhancement model;
  • visual examples showing the enhancement results;
  • comparisons between selected model settings;
  • an analysis of the strengths and limitations of the method; and
  • a complete undergraduate dissertation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing, or OFDM, is widely used in modern wireless communication systems, including Wi-Fi, 4G, and 5G. When an OFDM signal travels through a wireless channel, it may be affected by noise, reflections, and signal fading. As a result, the received symbols can be distorted and may be detected incorrectly.


A communication receiver normally uses an equaliser to reduce this distortion. Traditional equalisers are based on mathematical formulas and generally work well. However, neural networks provide another possible approach because they can learn how received signals are related to the original transmitted symbols.


This project will introduce the student to the basic idea of using a small neural network to assist signal equalisation in a simplified OFDM system. The work will focus on understanding, implementation, and visual comparison rather than developing a highly advanced communication system.


2. Main Tasks

  1. Learn the basic structure of an OFDM communication system.
  2. Use an existing Python or MATLAB example to simulate QPSK or 16-QAM transmission over a noisy wireless channel.
  3. Implement or reuse a simple conventional equaliser as a reference.
  4. Build a small neural network that receives distorted signal samples and produces corrected signal samples or detected symbols.
  5. Train the neural network using computer-generated data.
  6. Compare the conventional and neural-network methods using simple results such as:
  • constellation diagrams;
  • bit error rate;
  • training loss;
  • several example received signals.
  1. Discuss when the neural-network method works well and when it does not.

3. Expected Outcomes

The student is expected to produce:

  • a simple OFDM simulation in Python or MATLAB;
  • a basic conventional equaliser;
  • a small trained neural-network equaliser;
  • several clear plots showing the received signal before and after equalisation;
  • a simple comparison of bit error rate under a few noise conditions;
  • well-organised and commented source code;
  • a final-year dissertation describing the background, implementation, results, and conclusions.
rows.themeTitle: A Simple Neural Network Equaliser for OFDM Communication Systems

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Accurate channel estimation is one of the most important tasks in modern wireless communication systems. Before the receiver can correctly detect transmitted symbols, it must first estimate how the wireless channel has distorted the transmitted signal. Traditional channel estimation methods, such as Least Squares (LS) and Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE), have been widely adopted because of their simplicity and mathematical foundations. However, their performance can degrade significantly under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), fast time-varying channels, or highly complex propagation environments.


Recent advances in machine learning have demonstrated that neural networks can learn the relationship between received pilot signals and channel characteristics directly from data. Compared with conventional estimation methods, machine learning approaches have the potential to improve estimation accuracy while adapting more effectively to complicated wireless environments. As AI is expected to become an important enabling technology for future wireless networks, understanding its application to channel estimation represents an excellent entry point for undergraduate students interested in communication systems and artificial intelligence.


2. Main Tasks

  1. Conduct a literature review on conventional channel estimation techniques, including LS and MMSE estimators, together with recent machine learning-based channel estimation methods.
  2. Develop a simplified digital communication simulation platform in Python or MATLAB, including transmitter, wireless channel, pilot insertion, and receiver modules.
  3. Implement traditional LS and MMSE channel estimation algorithms as baseline methods.
  4. Design and train a lightweight machine learning model (such as a shallow neural network or fully connected network) to estimate the wireless channel using pilot observations.
  5. Compare the machine learning approach with conventional estimators under different SNR conditions and channel models, and analyse the advantages and limitations of both methods.

3. Expected Outcomes

The project is expected to produce:

  • A simulation platform for evaluating channel estimation algorithms.
  • Implementations of conventional LS/MMSE estimators and a machine learning-based estimator.
  • Performance comparisons under representative communication scenarios using metrics such as channel estimation error and bit error rate after equalisation.
  • A well-documented software package with clear instructions for reproducing the experiments.
  • A final undergraduate dissertation describing the background, methodology, implementation, experimental results, and conclusions.
rows.themeTitle: Machine Learning-based Channel Estimation for Digital Communication Systems

rows.themeProjectDescription:
This project focuses on efficient triggering for proactive LLM-based agents. Most current LLM-based agents are reactive, i.e., they stay idle until a user sends an explicit request, and then respond. A proactive agent, by contrast, continuously observes its context, e.g., incoming messages, calendar and file changes, an editor's activity, or the log of a long-running, and takes the initiative to offer help or perform an action at the right moment, without waiting to be asked. Typical examples include an assistant that notices an unanswered important email and drafts a reply, a coding assistant that spots a likely bug as the user types, or a monitoring agent that flags an anomaly in a running pipeline. Proactivity is what makes an agent feel genuinely helpful rather than a passive tool.

However, proactivity creates a serious efficiency problem. To be proactive, the agent must keep checking "is there anything I should do right now?", but in the overwhelming majority of moments the correct answer is "nothing." If the agent invokes a large language model on every event just to make this decision, the cost, latency, and compute become prohibitive, because genuine opportunities to act are sparse and most invocations are wasted. There is a trade-off between responsiveness (checking often enough not to miss a timely opportunity) and efficiency (not spending expensive reasoning on the many moments that need no action). This trade-off does not disappear with a more powerful model, as a stronger model only makes each unnecessary invocation more expensive, the key question is when it is worth invoking reasoning at all. Therefore, this project aims to study efficient triggering mechanisms for proactive agents, so that an agent can catch genuine opportunities to help while drastically reducing wasted invocations. The student is expected to complete the following tasks.

First, the student will review related work on proactive agents and proactive assistance, as well as efficiency techniques such as model cascades, lightweight routing/gating, and change/novelty detection, and identify a feasible technical route for an undergraduate final-year project. Second, the student will build a proactive-agent testbed: a stream of events or observations in a concrete scenario (for example incoming messages, editor or file events, or a task log), in which a small number of moments genuinely warrant a proactive action and most do not, with the trigger-worthy moments annotated as ground truth. Third, the student will implement a baseline proactive agent that invokes a large language model on every event to decide whether and how to act, serving as the expensive "always-on" reference. Fourth, the student will design and implement one or more efficient triggering mechanisms, e.g., a cheap gating stage (rule-based, embedding-similarity, or a small/cheap model) that escalates to the full LLM only when it detects a likely opportunity, together with strategies such as batching or debouncing events and skipping reasoning when the context has not changed materially. Fifth, the student will integrate the triggering mechanism with an open-source LLM model or a third-party LLM API to build a complete proactive-agent prototype that decides when to act and then produces the action or suggestion. Finally, the student will evaluate the system by comparing the always-on baseline with the efficient triggering strategies, producing a trade-off analysis between responsiveness (how many genuine opportunities are caught, and how timely) and efficiency (number of LLM invocations and latency), and also measuring the false-trigger rate.

The expected outputs include a proactive-agent testbed with annotated trigger moments, a baseline always-on agent, one or more efficient triggering mechanisms, a complete proactive-agent prototype, an efficiency–responsiveness trade-off analysis, and a complete final-year project dissertation.
rows.themeTitle: Towards Efficient Proactive LLM-based Agents

rows.themeProjectDescription:
This project focuses on workflow planning and orchestration for LLM-based agents. As large language models are increasingly used to automate multi-step tasks, an LLM-based agent is often asked to complete a complex job that involves several stages, such as gathering information, transforming data, calling external tools, summarizing intermediate results, and producing a final document. When such a task is handled with a single large prompt, the agent often loses track of intermediate steps, skips required operations, or produces unreliable results, because all reasoning, tool use, and output formatting are mixed together in one pass.

A more reliable approach is to organize a complex task as a workflow, a structured set of smaller, well-defined steps connected by their input and output dependencies, in which the language model is orchestrated step by step rather than asked to solve everything at once. The two central problems are planning, i.e., how to turn a user's natural-language request into a suitable workflow; and orchestration, i.e., how to execute that workflow correctly while managing intermediate state and handling failures. Writing a workflow by hand for every task is time-consuming, and a fixed workflow cannot adapt to different user requests. Therefore, this project aims to study how an LLM-based agent can automatically plan a workflow for a given task and then orchestrate its execution, thereby improving the reliability and controllability of multi-step task processing. The student is expected to complete the following tasks.

First, the student will review related work on LLM-based agents, common workflow patterns (such as prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, the orchestrator-worker pattern, and the evaluator-optimizer pattern), and task decomposition, and identify a feasible technical route for an undergraduate final-year project. Second, the student will design and implement a workflow representation, for example a directed acyclic graph or a JSON/YAML schema, that describes the steps of a task, their prompts or tool calls, and the data dependencies between them. Third, the student will implement a workflow planning module that uses an LLM to decompose a natural-language task into such a structured workflow, so that workflows do not have to be written entirely by hand. Fourth, the student will implement a workflow orchestration engine that resolves step dependencies, passes intermediate results between steps, supports sequential and simple parallel execution, and records the execution state. Fifth, the student will add an output-validation and error-recovery mechanism, so that the agent can check the result of a step, retry a failed step, or re-plan part of the workflow when necessary. Finally, the student will integrate these modules with an open-source LLM model or a third-party LLM API to build a simple LLM-based workflow agent prototype, and evaluate it on several multi-step tasks, comparing a single-prompt (monolithic) baseline, a hand-written workflow, and an automatically planned workflow in terms of task success rate, output quality, and robustness to failures.

The expected outputs include a workflow representation module, a workflow planning module, a workflow orchestration engine, an LLM-based workflow agent prototype, experimental analysis, and a complete final-year project dissertation.

1. Research Background

Quantum biology is rapidly converging with device engineering, opening a field where biological macromolecules serve as quantum-active components in next-generation neuro-photonic and quantum-effect hardware. Recent findings indicate that quantum coherence, tunneling, and associated spin dynamics not only govern energy and charge flow in photosynthetic complexes and enzymes but can also be harnessed within solid-state-like architectures. This project targets ferritin, luciferase, and related proteins as naturally evolved, nanoscale platforms for device integration. Ferritin’s 24-mer nanocage—which encapsulates an iron-oxide core resembling semiconductor quantum dots—exhibits gateable electron transfer relevant to neuronal clusters such as the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus. By embedding these proteins into metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) geometries and hybrid photonic waveguides, the project explores spin-selective transport, photon-mediated signaling, and room-temperature quantum coherence—phenomena fundamental to neuromorphic computing. Success will provide bio-derived channel materials for low-power quantum sensors, neuromorphic synapses, and implantable optoelectronic interfaces, positioning protein-based MOSFETs at the forefront of neuro-photonic circuits and quantum biotechnology.


2. Research Objectives

① Fundamental Objectives

Investigate how various organic and protein materials (including enzymes, ferritin nanocages, and related biomolecules) function as active channels within MOSFET architectures. Systematically optimize device geometries to achieve high carrier mobility, high on/off ratios, minimal energy consumption, and fully tunable organic/bio-hybrid transistors.

② Scope Expansion

Pursue targeted protein engineering to enhance device performance, focusing on biocompatibility for biosensing applications and stimulus-responsive behavior (e.g., light or humidity gating) for environmentally adaptive electronics.

③ Analytical Methods

Employ ultrafast spectroscopy—specifically transient absorption spectroscopy—to resolve charge-transfer dynamics within protein-based MOSFET channels and correlate these dynamics with macroscopic device characteristics.



3. Expected Objectives

a. Quantum-activated biomolecular channels

By utilizing ferritin, luciferase, and related proteins as the intrinsic semiconductor layer in MOSFETs, this project integrates quantum biological functions with established micro/nano-fabrication techniques. Unlike conventional organic semiconductors, these proteins possess naturally evolved quantum-confined cores and spin-selective pathways, offering a previously unexplored route to room-temperature quantum coherence and spin-polarized charge transport in solid-state devices.

b. Integration of neuro-photonic devices

Embedding protein-based channels into photonic waveguides and neuromorphic circuit layouts enables simultaneous electrical, optical, and spin-based readouts. This multimodal platform can emulate synaptic behavior, paving the way for implantable neuro-photonic processors and ultra-low-power brain-computer interfaces—capabilities currently unattainable with inorganic or purely organic electronics.

c. Stimuli-responsive and biodegradable electronics

Rational protein engineering will introduce light-, humidity-, or pH-activated switches, yielding environmentally adaptive transistors that are inherently biocompatible and biodegradable. Such devices can be printed on flexible substrates for temporary biomedical diagnostics or eco-friendly IoT nodes, thereby addressing the growing problem of electronic waste.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Wireless healthcare technologies are becoming increasingly important for patient monitoring, diagnosis, rehabilitation, and wearable medical systems. Antennas are a key component in these systems because they enable communication between sensors, medical devices, and external monitoring units. Healthcare antennas must be compact, lightweight, low-cost, safe for the human body, and able to operate reliably near lossy biological tissues. However, designing antennas for healthcare applications is challenging because the human body can detune the antenna, reduce radiation efficiency, and increase specific absorption rate (SAR). This project will investigate antenna designs suitable for wearable or body-centric healthcare applications, with a focus on improving performance, safety, and practical integration.


2. Main task

The main task of this FYP is to design, simulate, and evaluate a compact antenna for healthcare applications. The student will first review recent literature on wearable, implantable, and body-area-network antennas. Based on this review, suitable frequency bands such as ISM bands, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or 5G-related healthcare bands will be selected. The student will then design an antenna using electromagnetic simulation software such as CST, HFSS, or another suitable tool. The antenna performance will be quantified using parameters including reflection coefficient below −10 dB, bandwidth, gain, radiation efficiency, radiation pattern, and SAR. The effect of the human body or tissue-equivalent model will also be studied to understand antenna detuning and safety issues. Where possible, the design will be optimised to achieve compact size, stable operation, and SAR below standard safety limits.


3. Expected outcomes

By the end of the project, the student is expected to deliver a complete antenna design suitable for a healthcare-related application. The expected outcomes include a literature review, antenna geometry, simulation model, performance comparison, and technical discussion of the results. Quantified outcomes may include an operating frequency within the selected healthcare band, reflection coefficient below −10 dB, acceptable radiation efficiency, stable radiation pattern, and SAR compliance. The final report should clearly explain the design process, justify the selected parameters, compare the proposed design with existing work, and discuss possible future improvements such as fabrication, measurement, flexible substrates, or integration with wearable sensors.

rows.themePrerequisiteSkills:
I. Foundational

Knowledge


1. Optical Theory


Solid background in Geometrical Optics, including

Gaussian imaging formulas, paraxial optical systems, stops and aperture theory,

and aberration analysis, with the ability to design and analyze basic imaging

optical paths; Solid background in Physical Optics, with deep understanding of

core wave-optical concepts including interference, diffraction, and

polarization, capable of analyzing coherence and polarization effects in optical

systems; Solid background in Fourier Optics, mastering angular spectrum

propagation theory, spatial frequency analysis, the Fourier-transforming

property of lenses, and the interrelationship between Optical Transfer Function

(OTF) and Point Spread Function (PSF), with the ability to model and analyze

imaging systems using Fourier methods.

2. Software Proficiency


Proficiency in Matlab: capable of independently

writing numerical simulation programs for optical field propagation

calculations (e.g., angular spectrum method, Fresnel diffraction integral),

phase profile generation, image processing and quality assessment, and data

visualization; Proficiency in Zemax: capable of building imaging optical paths

in sequential mode, setting merit functions for phase profile optimization of

lenses/metasurfaces, and performing aberration analysis and tolerance analysis;

Proficiency in CST Studio Suite: capable of building periodic electromagnetic

simulation models, setting boundary conditions and excitation sources, executing

frequency-domain/time-domain solver simulations, performing parameter sweeps,

extracting S-parameters, and obtaining amplitude and phase response data of

unit cells.

3. Metasurface

Fundamentals


Understanding of basic operating principles of

metasurfaces, including the Generalized Snell's Law, Pancharatnam-Berry (P-B)

phase modulation mechanism, and Propagation Phase modulation mechanism; Understanding

of typical applications of metasurfaces in wavefront shaping, beam steering,

and lens imaging; Understanding of the mapping relationship between geometric

parameters (height, diameter, period, duty cycle) of metasurface unit

structures (e.g., nanopillars, nanofins, split-ring resonators) and their

optical responses (amplitude and phase).

II. Design Workflow


This project follows a complete R&D pipeline

of "theoretical design → numerical simulation → iterative optimization → experimental

fabrication → system

validation." The specific workflow is as follows:

Step 1: System Parameter

Pre-Design


Based on the application requirements of

high-resolution projection displays, determine the core design parameters of

the system, including: operating wavelength (λ, e.g., 532 nm green or 635 nm

red), target resolution (e.g., from 128×128 to 256×256 pixels), imaging geometry

(metasurface effective aperture and pixel size), projection distance (50–200

mm), resolution enhancement factor (2×2 or 3×3 stitching scheme), and

translation stepping precision (sub-pixel level). The output parameters of this

step serve as the boundary conditions for all subsequent design and simulation

stages.

Step 2: Metasurface Phase

Profile Optimization (Zemax)


Import the system parameters determined in Step 1

into Zemax to establish a complete projection optical model. Using minimization

of the Point Spread Function (PSF), minimization of wavefront error, or

maximization of the Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) as the optimization

goal, employ Zemax's sequential mode optimization functions to compute the

optimal phase profile φ(x, y) required for the metasurface. This phase profile

determines how the metasurface modulates the incident wavefront and is the core

element for achieving high-quality projection imaging.

Step 3: Unit Cell

Electromagnetic Simulation and Parameter Sweep (CST)


Build an electromagnetic simulation model of the

basic metasurface unit cell in CST Studio Suite. Design the unit cell geometry

(e.g., cylindrical nanopillars, square nanopillars), select substrate material

(e.g., SiO₂ or glass) and unit cell material (e.g., a-Si, TiO₂, or Si₃N₄). Set

periodic boundary conditions and plane-wave excitation, perform comprehensive

parameter sweeps over geometric parameters (height, diameter/side length,

period), and calculate the amplitude transmittance and phase delay for each

combination of geometric parameters. Finally, establish a complete

"structural parameters ↔ optical response" Look-Up Table (LUT) to

provide data support for subsequent unit cell arrangement.

Step 4: Inverse Mapping from

Phase Profile to Unit Cell Distribution and Layout Generation


Discretize and sample the continuous phase profile

φ(x, y) obtained in Step 2 according to the metasurface pixel grid. For each

discrete pixel position, search the LUT established in Step 3 to find the unit

cell geometric parameters whose phase value most closely matches the target and

whose amplitude transmittance is maximized, completing the inverse mapping from

phase to structure. Generate the complete metasurface layout based on the

matching results, exporting as a standardized GDSII format file or a custom

matrix format file for subsequent fabrication.

Step 5: Optical Propagation

Simulation and Image Reconstruction (Matlab)


Based on Fourier optics and angular spectrum

propagation theory, establish a numerical model of optical field propagation

through the metasurface in Matlab. Input the metasurface phase arrangement

generated in Step 4, simulate the outgoing optical field after metasurface

modulation and the imaging field distribution on the projection screen.

Simulate the sub-image projection results at different translational positions

of the metasurface (e.g., 4 positions in a 2×2 grid or 9 positions in a 3×3

grid), and use image stitching and super-resolution reconstruction algorithms

to fuse multiple low-resolution sub-frames into a single high-resolution image.

Calculate quality metrics of the reconstructed image including PSF, MTF,

contrast ratio, and SNR.

Step 6: Simulation Result

Analysis and Iterative Optimization


Perform a point-by-point comparative analysis between

the simulation outputs from Step 5 and the quantitative targets set in Step 1.

If any metric fails to meet the target, trace the error sources (possible

sources include phase discretization error, unit cell amplitude non-uniformity,

stitching misalignment error, insufficient diffraction efficiency, etc.) and

return to Step 2, Step 3, or Step 5 for targeted adjustments. Complete at least

two rounds of iterative optimization until all performance indicators satisfy

the design requirements.

Step 7: Metasurface Sample

Fabrication


Based on the GDSII layout file output from Step 4,

proceed with micro/nano fabrication either in-house or through a foundry

service. A typical process flow includes: substrate cleaning → EBL resist spin-coating

→ electron-beam lithography

(EBL) → development → reactive ion etching

(RIE) → resist stripping. After

fabrication, characterize the sample morphology using scanning electron

microscopy (SEM) to confirm that the dimensions and morphology of the unit

structures are consistent with the design layout.

Step 8: Experimental

Platform Construction and System Validation


Build a complete optical

testing platform comprising: a laser source (wavelength consistent with design)

→ beam expansion and collimation system → metasurface sample (mounted on a high-precision

piezoelectric translation stage) → projection screen → CMOS image acquisition camera. Write stage control and image

acquisition synchronization programs. According to the translation scheme

determined in Step 1, step the stage sequentially and capture low-resolution

sub-images at each position. Input the captured sub-image sequence into the

image stitching and reconstruction algorithm to obtain the final high-resolution

projected image. Compare the measured results (resolution, contrast ratio, MTF,

etc.) with simulation predictions to validate the correctness of the design and

analyze sources of experimental error.
rows.themeProjectDescription:
I. Introduction


Conventional projection display technologies have long relied

on spatial light modulators such as digital micromirror devices (DMDs) and

liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) panels, which modulate incident light pixel by

pixel to project images. As display resolutions advance from high-definition

toward 4K, 8K, and beyond, these technologies face increasingly severe

challenges: the continuous scaling of pixel size is not only constrained by the

physical limits of semiconductor manufacturing processes, but also leads to

reduced optical efficiency, increased thermal dissipation issues, and

drastically higher driving circuit complexity. Breaking through the resolution

bottleneck while maintaining system compactness and low cost has therefore become

a critical scientific challenge in the field of projection displays.

Metasurfaces—two-dimensional arrays of subwavelength unit

structures functioning as artificial electromagnetic interfaces—offer flexible

control over the amplitude, phase, and polarization of optical fields at

subwavelength scales, providing a brand-new platform for next-generation

ultra-thin projection optical systems. However, the space-bandwidth product of

a single metasurface is fundamentally limited by its physical pixel count, and

relying solely on fabrication process improvements to increase pixel density

faces the same trade-offs between cost and precision.

To address these challenges, this project proposes an

innovative scheme of "translationally reconfigurable metasurfaces":

by translating the metasurface with high-precision mechanical stages, multiple

frames of low-resolution sub-images are sequentially projected at different

spatial positions. Through sub-pixel image stitching and super-resolution

reconstruction algorithms, these sub-frames are fused into a single

high-resolution image. The core philosophy of this approach is "trading

time for space"—sacrificing temporal sampling to achieve spatial

resolution beyond the physical pixel limit, without requiring any advancement

in fabrication technology. This strategy synergistically integrates the

subwavelength light-field modulation capability of metasurfaces, the

multi-frame fusion theory of computational imaging, and precision displacement

control techniques, opening up a new pathway for developing ultra-compact,

low-cost, and reconfigurable high-resolution projection systems. This research

aims to establish a complete technical framework encompassing theoretical

design, simulation optimization, and experimental validation, thereby advancing

the practical application of reconfigurable metasurfaces in dynamic displays.

II. Main Task


The primary tasks of this project span the entire chain of

"design—simulation—fabrication—validation," and specifically include

the following core components: System parameter design and quantitative

specification: Define key parameters including operating wavelength, target

resolution, projection distance, and field of view based on application

requirements. Determine the resolution enhancement factor (target: 4×

enhancement, from 128×128 to 256×256 pixels) and the corresponding translation

stepping scheme.

Metasurface phase profile optimization: Build a projection

optical model in Zemax based on system parameters, and solve for the optimal

phase profile of the metasurface by minimizing the point spread function and

wavefront error.

Unit cell electromagnetic simulation and database construction:

Establish the basic unit cell model of the metasurface in CST, perform

parameter sweeps to obtain amplitude transmittance and phase delay data for

varying geometric dimensions, and construct a comprehensive

"structure—optical response" lookup table.

Inverse mapping from phase to structure and layout

generation: Discretize the theoretically optimized phase profile, match each

pixel to the nearest available unit structure from the database, and generate a

fabricable metasurface layout file.

Numerical simulation of optical propagation and image

reconstruction: Based on Fourier optics and angular spectrum propagation

theory, simulate the projected imaging results of the metasurface at each

translational position using Matlab, reconstruct the high-resolution image via

multi-frame stitching algorithms, and compute quality metrics such as MTF and

contrast ratio.

Iterative optimization: Based on simulation feedback,

iteratively refine the phase profile, unit cell structures, and stitching

algorithms to ensure all performance specifications meet the design targets.

Metasurface sample fabrication: Fabricate the metasurface

sample on transparent substrates using micro/nano-fabrication processes

including electron-beam lithography and reactive ion etching, followed by

scanning electron microscopy characterization.

Experimental platform construction and system validation:

Build an optical testing system comprising a laser source, beam collimation

optics, a high-precision piezoelectric translation stage, and a CMOS camera.

Conduct actual translation-projection imaging experiments to validate the

consistency between simulation results and real-system performance.

III. Expected Results


The core focus of this research lies in the functional

realization and performance validation of translationally reconfigurable

metasurface projection displays, with technical significance manifested in the

following aspects: In terms of imaging resolution, through multi-frame

sub-pixel translational stitching, the spatial resolution of the projected

image is expected to be enhanced by a factor of 4 (2×2 stitching) or 9 (3×3

stitching) relative to the physical pixel count, thereby demonstrating the

feasibility and effectiveness of the "trading time for space"

strategy in metasurface-based display systems. In terms of imaging quality, the

reconstructed images are expected to achieve a contrast ratio exceeding 10:1

and a modulation transfer function no lower than 0.3 at the target resolution,

ensuring clear edges and rich fine details.

In terms of device performance, the designed metasurface unit

structures are expected to exhibit transmittance of no less than 60% and full

2π phase coverage, providing the foundation for high-efficiency light-field

modulation. In terms of system integration, a complete technical workflow

spanning theoretical design (Zemax + CST + Matlab), micro/nano fabrication, and

optical testing will be established, laying the groundwork for future system

miniaturization and dynamic reconfiguration.

Building upon these research outcomes, the translationally

reconfigurable metasurface projection technology holds promise for future

applications in the following scenarios: (1) ultra-compact portable projectors,

leveraging the ultra-thin planar nature of metasurfaces to dramatically reduce

projection engine volume, suitable for wearable displays and mobile smart

devices; (2) augmented reality displays, serving as compact light engines for

high-resolution image projection; (3) computational imaging systems, combined

with the dynamic tunability of reconfigurable metasurfaces to achieve

switchable resolution and field-of-view adaptive projection displays. The

successful implementation of this project will provide critical theoretical

foundations and experimental support for the interdisciplinary convergence of

novel flat-panel display technologies and dynamic metasurface modulation

techniques.

（1）Background

Piezoelectric materials are core functional components in micro-energy harvesting, flexible sensors, MEMS actuators and wearable electronic devices, showing great application value in industrial monitoring and consumer electronics. Traditional bulk piezoelectric materials are limited by high brittleness and poor shape adaptability, while piezoelectric composites prepared by liquid polymer matrix curing have the advantages of low cost, simple process, good flexibility and customizable morphology. Currently, PZT (lead zirconate titanate) is the most widely used piezoelectric filler with outstanding piezoelectric performance; BTO (barium titanate) is a representative lead-free piezoelectric material with excellent environmental compatibility; ZnO (zinc oxide) has the characteristics of low cost, easy synthesis and stable chemical properties. However, there is still a lack of systematic comparative study on the piezoelectric properties of these three materials under completely consistent preparation and polarization conditions in the same liquid matrix system. This project carries out controlled variable experiments to fill this research gap and provide data reference for the selection of piezoelectric fillers in flexible composite systems.

（2）Main Task

1. Prepare three groups of piezoelectric composite samples by doping PZT, BTO and ZnO particles into the same liquid epoxy resin matrix respectively, with strictly consistent filler mass fraction, mixing process, curing temperature and curing time.

2. Optimize the polarization process parameters (polarization electric field strength, polarization temperature and holding time), and perform high-voltage polarization treatment on all cured samples under unified conditions.

3. Test and characterize key performance parameters of the three samples, including piezoelectric strain constant d33, relative dielectric constant, dielectric loss, electromechanical coupling coefficient and cycle stability of piezoelectric response.

4. Conduct comparative analysis on the performance differences of the three composites, and explain the internal mechanism combined with microstructure characterization results.

（3）Expected Outcomes

1. Obtain complete and reliable comparative data of piezoelectric and dielectric properties for PZT, BTO and ZnO polymer matrix composites.

2. Clarify the performance advantages, limitations and applicable scenarios of the three piezoelectric fillers in liquid curing matrix systems.

3. Summarize a set of standardized preparation and polarization process scheme for liquid-based piezoelectric composite materials.

4. Complete a full graduation design thesis containing complete experimental data, mechanism analysis and research conclusions, meeting the academic requirements of the final year project.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Deep Learning (DL) models have been successfully used for different audio processing tasks. This project explores the capability of state-of-the-art DL methods to process animal sounds via filtering, recognizing, classifying, and translating audio signals. Animals do not speak in continuous audio, having inconsistent and varied-length pauses, different accents, and phonetic variations. The primary goal is to replicate/develop DL models that overcome these challenges for filtering, recognizing, classifying, and translating animal audio signals. The project will use open-source datasets and implement existing data augmentation techniques to enhance the model accuracy. The project will also involve a comparison with other baseline methods to evaluate performance. Overall, the project will include the following 4 subtasks:

1) Animal sounds filtering, processing, and classification using available open-source datasets

2) Animal sounds recognition and signal isolation in noisy conditions using open-source datasets

3) Animal sounds classification tasks over heterogeneous open-source audio datasets

4) Audio to text and language detection over open-source animal sound datasets

1. Background


The growing demand for higher wireless capacity has driven interest in visible light as a complementary spectrum for 6G systems. Visible light offers massive unlicensed bandwidth and can be used for both illumination and high-speed data transmission. This project theme aims to design and implement a practical 10 Mbps LiFi system based on visible light for indoor internet access.

The three sub-projects are deliberately structured around the classic communication system blocks, i,e., theoretical modelling & simulation, transmitter hardware, and receiver hardware, which enables a high degree of parallel development with relatively low interdependence until the final integration and testing phase.


2. Main tasks


Project Title 1: Link Budget Analysis, Channel Modelling and End-to-end Simulation of 10 Mbps VLC Communication Links

This sub-project focuses on the theoretical and simulation aspects. Students will perform detailed link budget analysis, model the optical wireless channel, conduct end-to-end simulations (including modulation, noise, and impairments), and establish the system specifications and performance targets for the 10 Mbps LiFi prototype.


Project Title 2: High-speed LED Driver Design, Implementation and Experimental Characterisation (Transmitter Side)

This sub-project focuses on the transmitter hardware. Students will design and implement high-speed LED driver circuits capable of supporting 10 Mbps modulation, perform PSpice simulation, PCB layout, board assembly, and conduct thorough experimental characterisation of the optical transmitter performance (rise time, bandwidth, linearity, etc.).


Project Title 3: High-speed Optical Receiver Design and Implementation (Transimpedance Amplifier and Signal Conditioning)

This sub-project focuses on the receiver hardware. Students will design and implement a high-speed transimpedance amplifier (TIA) and subsequent signal conditioning stages, optimise for noise, bandwidth and dynamic range, carry out simulation and PCB implementation, and experimentally characterise the optical receiver performance.


3. Expected outcomes


The key deliverables include theoretical analysis, simulation validation, and analogue circuit implementation, specifically the LED driver and the receiving transimpedance amplifier. Ultimately, an initial prototype supporting point-to-point connections will be developed. Depending on progress and time availability, enhancements for point-to-multipoint support may also be explored.

1. Background 


PV solar cells are traditionally used only for energy harvesting. However, their inherent photosensitivity also enables them to detect modulated optical signals, offering the potential for simultaneous energy harvesting and low-bandwidth optical wireless communication. This dual functionality is particularly attractive for creating energy-autonomous IoT devices in indoor environments.

This project theme investigates the co-design of energy harvesting and optical communication using commercial PV solar cells. The three sub-projects address different technical layers — device characterisation and modelling, analogue front-end circuit design, and embedded communication protocols — allowing students to work with a high degree of independence while contributing to the same overall goal of sustainable VLC-IoT systems.


2. Main tasks



Project Title 1: Experimental Characterisation and Multi-domain Modelling of PV Solar Cells for Dual Energy-Communication Functionality

This sub-project focuses on systematic experimental characterisation of PV solar cells, including I-V curves, optical responsivity, frequency response, and efficiency under various lighting conditions. Students will develop automated measurement scripts and establish accurate models that capture the trade-offs between energy harvesting and communication capability.


Project Title 2: Design and Optimisation of Power-Signal Decoupling and Front-end Circuits for PV-based Optical Receivers

This sub-project focuses on analogue circuit design. Students will design and implement specialised decoupling circuits that separate the DC power path (for energy harvesting) from the AC signal path (for data reception), optimise noise performance and bandwidth, and validate the circuits through simulation and PCB prototyping.


Project Title 3: Energy-aware Communication Protocols and Firmware Development for Self-powered VLC-IoT Nodes

This sub-project focuses on the embedded systems and protocol layer. Students will design lightweight communication protocols and firmware suitable for energy-constrained PV-powered IoT nodes, implement data decoding and power management strategies, and evaluate performance in terms of energy efficiency and communication reliability (can be tested with commercial PV cells and existing decoupling circuits).


3. Expected outcomes


A theoretical analysis of the PV solar cell's electrical characteristics will be conducted as the basis for its further use as a dual-functionality component for both energy harvesting and wireless communication. To achieve the optimal point for both functionalities, a trade-off discussion is expected. With the theoretical analysis ready, a hardware implementation demo is expected to be delivered.

1 Background


Indoor positioning achieving a comparable accuracy to outdoor GPS positioning has been challenging for decades. Due to significant attenuation of GPS signals inside buildings, current indoor positioning mainly relies on indoor short-range RF technologies like UWB (e.g. Apple AirTags), WiFi or Bluetooth. To be precise, these existing RF solutions suffer from limited accuracy and repeatability, thus on most occasions provide a poor positional resolution, limiting the use of indoor tracking. The emerging VLC/LiFi technologies offer a promising alternative to RF approaches. In a typical indoor environment, existing luminaries are based on solid-state LEDs, and they can be converted into light beacons with minor changes to the LED driver, enabling a cost-effective infrastructure upgrade without resource waste.


2 Main tasks


This project theme focuses on developing key enabling technologies for practical VLC-based indoor localisation. Students will work on the design and characterisation of optical beacon transmitters, as well as the development of robust decoding and geometry-based localisation algorithms suitable for mobile devices. The two sub-projects are designed to be largely independent, allowing parallel development, while their outputs can be combined in the final demonstration phase.


Project Title 1: Design, Implementation and Experimental Characterisation of VLC Beacon Transmitter Hardware

This sub-project focuses on the hardware aspects of the system. Students will design programmable LED drivers capable of modulating luminaires to broadcast unique beacon IDs, implement the beacon frame structure in hardware/firmware, and conduct comprehensive experimental characterisation of optical transmission performance under realistic indoor conditions.


Project Title 2: Development of Robust Beacon Decoding and Geometry-based Localisation Algorithms for Mobile Platforms

This sub-project focuses on the algorithmic and software aspects. Students will develop reliable beacon decoding methods from camera images or photodetector signals, design and implement geometry-based localisation algorithms (triangulation, multilateration, etc.), and validate performance through simulation and offline processing of real or synthetic data. The algorithms can be later integrated with the hardware from Project Title 1 for real-time demonstration.


3 Expected outcomes

A complete demo system is expected. The hardware part includes an LED driver which can be programmed to transmit customised beacon IDs. The software part, ideally, is expected to be delivered as an Android app which can capture images, decode luminare's beacon IDs, and calculate the user's geometrical localisation in real time.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background Mobile banking apps increasingly use face recognition to authenticate users. A face check is only safe if the system can confirm the camera is seeing a live person rather than a photo, a replayed video, or a mask — a problem known as face liveness detection. As phone cameras and consumer media tools improve, simple spoofing attempts (printed photos, screen replays) are easy to attempt, so banking apps need a liveness layer that is accurate, fast on ordinary phones, privacy-respecting, and aligned with recognised testing standards. This is a civilian, consumer-facing anti-fraud problem built entirely on publicly available datasets, open-source tools, and published methods.

2. Main task Students will design, implement, and evaluate a complete face-liveness pipeline for a banking-style mobile app, from camera input to a live/not-live decision, with on-device, privacy-by-design operation. The theme is engineering-led: each student creates and justifies design decisions, evaluates alternatives, and validates performance against recognised benchmarks (e.g. the iBeta / ISO/IEC 30107-3 presentation-attack-detection testing philosophy) rather than only applying an off-the-shelf model.

3. Expected outcomes A working, documented liveness-detection prototype (model + mobile integration), a reproducible evaluation harness, measured accuracy/latency/model-size trade-offs across phones, and a design rationale covering security-versus-usability, privacy, and standards compliance.

Division of labour (independent objectives, minimal overlap):

  • S1 — Mobile face detection & preprocessing front-end. Design a fast, robust face-detection and alignment stage (OpenCV/MediaPipe) tuned for low-power phones; characterise latency vs accuracy.
  • S2 — Liveness classification model. Design and train a CNN live/not-live classifier on public datasets (e.g. CASIA-FASD, Replay-Attack, OULU-NPU); justify architecture choices and evaluate.
  • S3 — Robustness to print & replay attacks. Engineer texture/frequency/motion features to separate live faces from 2-D photo and screen-replay attempts; evaluate detection performance.
  • S4 — Model compression for deployment. Apply quantisation, pruning, and distillation for TensorFlow Lite; measure model-size vs accuracy trade-offs.
  • S5 — Cross-device performance evaluation. Build a test harness assessing consistency across phone types, camera qualities, and OSs, with uncertainty analysis.
  • S6 — Generalisation evaluation framework. Design a cross-dataset protocol to test how well the system handles attack types unseen during training.
  • S7 — Banking app integration & user experience. Build the front-end app (React Native/Flutter) integrating the model; tune the security threshold (FAR/FRR) against usability.
  • S8 — Standards, privacy & compliance-by-design. Map the system to iBeta Level 2 / ISO/IEC 30107 testing and GDPR privacy-by-design (on-device inference, data minimisation); analyse societal, ethical, and commercial impact.

Emerging technologies such as Virtual Reality (VR), Extended Reality (XR), Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), and multimodal analytics are transforming the future of education and professional training. Intelligent immersive learning environments can provide personalised, interactive, and emotionally responsive learning experiences that enhance learner engagement, motivation, and knowledge retention. This project theme focuses on the design and development of AI-powered immersive learning systems that integrate virtual environments, conversational AI, emotion and engagement recognition, and real-time learning analytics. Students will develop a platform that improves human learning experiences while gaining hands-on experience in artificial intelligence, computer vision, signal processing, human-computer interaction, and immersive technologies.


Project 1: Generative AI for 360° Immersive Learning Environment Creation

rows.themeProjectDescription:
This overarching project theme bridges the critical gap between atomistic material behaviour and macroscopic electromagnetic phenomena. Situated at the cutting edge of nanoscale engineering, the project tasks students with coupling Molecular Dynamics (MD) with Discontinuous Galerkin Time-Domain (DGTD) solvers to investigate the terahertz near-field plasmonic responses of advanced 2D materials, including graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), and hybrid perovskites.


The core objective is to decode how environmental stressors, surface degradation, and transient charge transport alter local dielectric properties, as these factors directly dictate the reliability and sensitivity of biosensing platforms.


Beyond the technical research, the project is structurally designed to cultivate rigorous scientific computing and resilient problem-solving. Students will utilise open-source computational workflows.


--

Sub-project 1: Investigating the Electrical Conductivity of 2D Materials in Ambient Conditions


Aim: To determine how environmental factors, specifically humidity, alter the local THz dielectric properties of graphene using a coupled Molecular Dynamics (MD) and Discontinuous Galerkin Time-Domain (DGTD) approach.


Tasks:

  1. Configure and execute MD simulations (e.g., using LAMMPS) to model water molecule adsorption onto a graphene lattice.
  2. Extract the modified local dielectric functions and conductivity parameters from the resulting MD trajectories.
  3. Import these parameters into a DGTD solver to simulate the modified THz near-field plasmonic response.


Outcomes:


  1. A functional multiscale model mapping varying humidity levels to specific changes in THz response.
  2. A fully documented, reproducible simulation workflow that links MD outputs to DGTD inputs.
  3. A finalised report detailing the relationship between ambient moisture and graphene's plasmonic behavior.


--


Sub-project 2: Analysing Surface Degradation Effects in Anisotropic 2D Materials


Aim: To quantify the impact of surface oxidation and structural degradation on the anisotropic THz near-field response of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDCs like MoS₂ or WSe₂).


Tasks:


  1. Model surface oxidation and air-induced degradation of TMDCs using MD to generate spatially varying, degraded anisotropic permittivity tensors.
  2. Map these anisotropic tensors into a DGTD solver, ensuring the solver is configured to handle the directional asymmetry of the degraded 2D lattice.
  3. Simulate the THz scattering efficiency and extract near-field maps of the degraded models.
  4. Compare the DGTD simulation outputs against provided experimental measurements of standard exfoliated TMDC samples.


Outcomes:


  1. A validated computational model demonstrating how TMDC degradation mechanisms manifest in THz near-field optics.
  2. Quantitative assessment of sensor stability and performance variation under oxidative stress.
  3. A comparative analysis document highlighting the alignment and discrepancies between the simulated anisotropic models and experimental data.


--


Sub-project 3: Understanding Charge Transport in 2D Materials through Transient THz Imaging


Aim: To model and identify the signatures of transient charge transport and mobility degradation in 2D perovskites using time-domain THz simulations.


Tasks:


  1. Simulate ion migration and ultra-fast carrier dynamics in 2D perovskite structures using MD.
  2. Translate the MD-derived transient carrier transport maps into time-dependent inputs for the DGTD solver.
  3. Execute time-domain simulations to capture the ultra-fast THz near-field signals, avoiding the limitations of frequency-domain solvers for complex temporal dynamics.


Outcomes:


  1. Detailed transient THz profiles characterising charge transport and mobility in 2D perovskites.
  2. A refined, peer-reviewed simulation codebase capable of handling complex temporal electrodynamics.
  3. Identification of specific THz signatures that correspond to known degradation processes in perovskite materials.


--


Sub-project 4: Evaluating Standard Harmonic Demodulation Techniques for THz Near-Field Data


Aim: To benchmark, optimize, and automate harmonic demodulation and background suppression algorithms for the post-processing of THz s-SNOM experimental data.


Tasks:

  1. Develop automated processing scripts (using C or Python) to execute lock-in amplification and harmonic demodulation on raw data arrays.
  2. Process provided benchmark experimental datasets (e.g., doped Silicon) through the newly developed scripting pipeline.
  3. Iteratively evaluate and adjust the scripts to maximize signal-to-noise ratio, enhance spatial resolution, and suppress near-field artefacts.


Outcomes:


  1. An optimised, automated, and well-commented C/Python processing pipeline for raw s-SNOM data.
  2. Clear, quantitative metrics defining the algorithm's performance under varying signal and noise conditions.
  3. A comprehensive presentation evaluating the effectiveness of standard post-processing techniques in recovering pure near-field THz signals.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
This theme offers a rigorous exploration into advanced time-domain electrodynamics, bridging the gap between theoretical physics and computational engineering. It enables final-year students to move beyond commercial, black-box software by developing, interrogating, and optimising their own numerical solvers to simulate complex nanoscale light-matter interactions.


Project 1: Time-Domain Simulation of Anisotropic Metamaterials


Background: Metamaterials and transformation optics enable the spatial routing of electromagnetic fields around an object, effectively reconfiguring the field as desired. Standard orthogonal simulation meshes struggle to resolve these curved, complex geometries without inducing non-physical numerical artefacts (stair-casing).


Task: Students will implement a two-dimensional Discontinuous Galerkin Time-Domain (DGTD) solver. The primary computational challenge involves extending the basic isotropic formulation to support and accurately process two-dimensional anisotropic permittivity tensors.


Outcome: The final deliverable is a validated total-field/scattered-field (TF/SF) map demonstrating a canonical shape around which the electromagnetic fields can be reconfigured.


--


Project 2: FDTD Modelling of Cathodoluminescence and SPP Modes in Nanowires


Background: When a high-energy electron beam interacts with a metallic nanostructure, it acts as a highly localised, moving current source. This dynamic excitation couples into the metal, generating surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) that propagate along the structure and emit radiation.


Task: Utilising custom Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) simulations, students will model the permittivity of a metal using a time-dependent polarisation based on Lorentz fitting parameters. They will simulate the electron impact as a short pulse of an electric field applied to the surface of a silver nanowire (specifically 60 nm in diameter and 1.8 um in length).


Outcome: Students must extract the longitudinal electric field as a function of time, mapping the single mode that propagates to the ends of the wire and reflects back.


--


Project 3: Retardation Effects and the Breakdown of the Quasi-Static Limit


Background: In sub-wavelength optics, the quasi-static approximation assumes that the phase of the incident electromagnetic field is uniform across a nanoparticle. However, as particle sizes increase, electromagnetic retardation and radiation damping disrupt this electrostatic assumption, altering resonant frequencies and scattering profiles.


Task: Student will utilise three-dimensional DGTD methodologies, leveraging high-order basis functions to accurately resolve strong field gradients around bar- and V-shaped metallic nanostructures on dielectric substrates. They will execute automated length-scaling sweeps from 15 nm up to 200 nm.


Outcome: Student will generate analytical plots mapping the specific critical size which determines the onset of the quasi-static limit, and highlight the significant deviations from quasi-static theory.


--


Project 4: Coherent Control of Nano-Antenna Hotspots via Chirped Pulses


Background: Tailored optical pulses offer a mechanism to dynamically manipulate particle plasmon resonances. By varying the instantaneous frequency of an excitation pulse over time (chirping), it is possible to control the constructive and destructive interference of the localised fields at the nanoscale.


Task: This project focuses on simulating the transient response of silver V-shaped nano-antennas to frequency-chirped femtosecond pulses. Student will write scripts to systematically tune the chirp parameters to investigate the limits of coherent control schemes.


Outcome: The expected outcome is a computational pipeline that identifies optimised chirp parameters to maximise spatio-temporal localisation of radiation in conjunction with large field enhancements at the antenna apex.

This project theme focuses on developing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven solutions for detecting, monitoring, and analyzing subsea environments, particularly in relation to marine pollution (e.g., plastic and waste) and marine life monitoring. With the growing demand for environmental sustainability and underwater ecosystem protection, students will explore applications such as object detection, marine debris identification, and marine life classification using AI techniques.


  1. AI-Based Detection of Marine Plastic Waste in Underwater Images: This project uses AI/computer vision to detect plastic waste such as bottles, bags, and wrappers in underwater images.It helps support marine pollution monitoring by automatically identifying harmful plastic materials in subsea environments.
  2. Marine Debris Classification Using Artificial Intelligence: This project focuses on classifying different types of marine debris, such as plastic, metal, glass, fishing gear, and general waste. It can help researchers understand the type and quantity of pollution present in underwater ecosystems.
  3. AI-Based Jellyfish Species Classification for Subsea Monitoring: This project uses image classification techniques to identify different jellyfish species from underwater images.It is useful for monitoring jellyfish populations, studying marine biodiversity, and detecting species changes in the ocean.

  5. Marine Shell and Snail Shell Recognition Using Artificial Intelligence: This project uses deep learning to recognize and classify marine shells and snail shells from image datasets.It can help with species identification, marine biodiversity documentation, and ecological monitoring.
  6. Underwater Image Enhancement for Improving Marine Object Detection: This project improves the quality of underwater images affected by poor lighting, blur, haze, or colour distortion. Enhanced images can improve the accuracy of AI models used for detecting marine life, plants, and pollution.
  7. AI Dashboard for Monitoring Marine Pollution and Marine Life from Underwater Images: This project develops a dashboard to display AI results such as detected waste, marine life types, confidence scores, and image summaries. It helps users visualize subsea monitoring data and understand environmental conditions more easily.
  8. AI-Based Seagrass Detection and Classification for Marine Ecosystem Monitoring: This project uses AI to detect and classify seagrass or underwater plants from marine images. Seagrass is important because it provides habitat for marine life, improves water quality, and acts as an indicator of ecosystem health.

rows.themeProjectDescription: In increasingly complex electromagnetic spectrum environments, to achieve control over spectrum resources, it is first necessary to determine whether the radiation source emitting a signal is a known friendly entity. To address this problem, this graduation project studied an algorithm based on the ratio of computational feature subspace projections. Known-class feature representations are obtained through neural networks; subsequently, two orthogonal subspaces of the known-class feature matrix are derived. Using the ratio of feature projections within these two subspaces as a metric, a decision is made on whether a radiation source signal sample belongs to a known class. The graduation project requires completing the study of this algorithm, implementing simulations on open datasets, and finishing the graduation thesis.
