rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background:

The natural environment is changing rapidly across many dimensions simultaneously: soil moisture and groundwater are declining, permafrost and glacial ice are thawing, desertification is spreading, wildfires are becoming longer and more destructive, and the terrestrial carbon cycle is being disrupted by land use change and vegetation loss, yet existing monitoring networks based on isolated point sensors and infrequent satellite observations cannot provide the continuous, spatially resolved measurements needed to understand and manage these processes at the scales that matter. Radio frequency tomography offers a compelling solution to this challenge: when radio waves travel through or across the ground, their amplitude, phase, and polarisation are modified in characteristic and measurable ways by the dielectric properties of the materials they encounter, meaning that soil moisture, ice content, organic matter concentration, vegetation water stress, and the dryness of combustible fuel can all be inferred by deploying a network of transmitting and receiving antenna nodes and mathematically reconstructing the spatial distribution of dielectric properties from the received signal patterns. This project exploits that principle through design and characterisation of advanced ground-penetrating radar and metasurface-loaded compact antennas and development of an RF soil moisture and hydrological monitoring system, an RF wildfire early warning system, an RF approach to estimating carbon stocks in soils, peatlands, and forest biomass to deliver a unified, low-power, autonomous environmental RF sensing platform.


Theme 1:Advanced Antenna Design for RF Environmental Tomography Ground-Penetrating Radar and Metasurface Antennas

Main Tasks:

  1. Review the electromagnetic properties of all target media across the environments covered by the project and identify the frequency ranges and measurement configurations that provide the best sensitivity for each monitoring application. 
  2. Design and optimise both antenna types, the wideband ground-penetrating radar antenna and the compact metasurface-loaded antenna, through full-wave electromagnetic simulation, targeting efficient coupling into the ground, adequate bandwidth, and controlled near-field radiation pattern. 
  3. Fabricate both antenna prototypes and characterise their performance in a laboratory setting, comparing simulated and measured results and refining the designs where necessary. 
  4. Validate both antennas in a representative outdoor field environment against commercial reference antennas, and deliver the characterised designs together with integration specifications ready for substitution into the monitoring systems of Themes 2, 3, and 4.


Expected Outcomes:

  • A wideband GPR antenna prototype optimised for subsurface environmental sensing, fully characterised in simulation and measurement
  • A compact metasurface-loaded antenna prototype demonstrating improved size-to-performance ratio relative to a commercial reference antenna
  • A validated simulation workflow enabling rapid re-optimisation of both antenna types for different media and deployment scenarios
  • A comprehensive antenna characterisation report with simulation and measurement comparisons across all target media
  • An integration datasheet specifying the electrical, mechanical, and software interfaces required for substitution into the Theme 2, 3, and 4 monitoring systems


Theme 2: RF-Based Soil Moisture and Hydrological Monitoring Across Contrasting Land Environments

Main Tasks:

  1. Review the electromagnetic properties of the target soil types across the range of moisture, temperature, and compositional conditions expected in each environment, and select the measurement frequencies and system configuration that provide the best sensitivity to subsurface hydrological state. 
  2. Develop and validate the RF measurement and signal inversion system in a controlled laboratory setting with known soil conditions, establishing the core workflow for converting raw RF measurements into spatially resolved subsurface moisture maps using AI-based inversion and pattern recognition algorithms trained on the laboratory dataset. 
  3. Deploy and validate the monitoring system in the target field environments, collecting co-located reference measurements for algorithm calibration, and using AI to assess and continuously improve the sensitivity of the system to seasonal and climatic variability across contrasting land types.
  4. Make the system ready to be integrated with the advanced antenna designs from Theme 1 into the validated monitoring system and quantify the improvement in performance relative to the commercial antenna baseline used throughout the development phase (if the design is ready).


Expected Outcomes:

  • A validated RF-based soil moisture and hydrology monitoring system demonstrated across at least two contrasting land environment types
  • Calibrated signal inversion and tomographic reconstruction algorithms converting RF measurements to spatially resolved subsurface moisture maps
  • A characterised performance comparison between the commercial antenna baseline system and the integrated Theme 1 advanced antenna system
  • A dataset of co-located RF measurements and reference soil moisture observations suitable for algorithm development and community sharing
  • A report documenting the sensitivity, accuracy, and limitations of the RF approach in each target environment


Theme 3: RF-Based Wildfire Early Warning Through Soil and Vegetation Drying Detection

 Main Tasks:

  1. Review the electromagnetic properties of soils, surface litter, and vegetation across a range of moisture and dryness conditions, and identify the measurement frequencies and propagation configurations that are most sensitive to the drying signatures relevant to wildfire ignition risk. 
  2. Develop and validate the RF drying detection system in a controlled outdoor environment using commercial antenna hardware, collecting co-located reference moisture measurements to establish the relationship between RF signal changes and progressive drying of soil and vegetation. 
  3. Deploy the system in a fire-prone landscape, collect continuous RF measurements alongside standard fire weather observations, and develop and train an AI-based classification algorithm that maps the spatial distribution of drying state and generates an autonomous, continuously updated fire risk indicator from the measured RF data. 
  4. Quantify the drying detection sensitivity and spatial coverage and assess the robustness of the AI classifier against environmental variables such as wind, rain, and temperature fluctuation that could affect system reliability.
  5. Make the system ready to be integrated with the advanced antenna designs from Theme 1 into the validated monitoring system and quantify the improvement in performance relative to the commercial antenna baseline used throughout the development phase (if the design is ready).


Expected Outcomes:

  • A validated RF-based wildfire early warning system demonstrating reliable detection of critical soil and vegetation drying conditions in a field environment
  • A calibrated signal inversion and fire risk classification algorithm benchmarked against standard fire weather indices and direct fuel moisture measurements
  • A characterised dataset of RF drying signatures across a range of soil types, vegetation types, and weather conditions
  • A report assessing the feasibility of large-scale deployment of the RF early warning network in fire-prone landscapes



Theme 4: RF-Based Carbon Stock Monitoring in Soils, Peatlands, and Forest Biomass

Main Tasks:

 

  1. Review the electromagnetic properties of organic-rich soils, peatlands, and forest biomass across a range of moisture and compositional conditions, and identify the measurement frequencies and configurations that provide the greatest sensitivity to carbon content independently of moisture variability. 
  2. Develop and validate the RF carbon sensing system in a controlled laboratory setting using soil and peat samples of known composition, and develop an AI-based inversion model trained on the laboratory data to separate the carbon signal from the confounding effects of moisture and bulk density. 
  3. Deploy the monitoring system in target field environments covering both soil and peat carbon and forest biomass applications, collect co-located reference measurements for AI model calibration and validation, and benchmark the RF-derived carbon estimates against established carbon stock assessment methods. 
  4. Make the system ready to be integrated with the advanced antenna designs from Theme 1 into the validated monitoring system and quantify the improvement in performance relative to the commercial antenna baseline used throughout the development phase (if the design is ready).


Expected Outcomes:

  • A validated RF-based soil organic carbon and peat depth estimation system, demonstrated in at least one field environment against independent geochemical reference measurements
  • A validated above-ground forest biomass estimation method based on RF propagation measurements, benchmarked against forest inventory data
  • Calibrated inversion algorithms separating the effects of organic carbon content, moisture, and bulk density on the measured RF dielectric response
  • A report quantifying the uncertainty and spatial resolution of the RF carbon stock estimates in the target environments

Background:

Monitoring the health of patients continuously and reliably outside of hospital settings is one of the most important challenges in modern healthcare. Chronic conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, and neurological disorders cause the majority of premature deaths worldwide and place a heavy burden on healthcare systems that cannot keep patients under constant clinical supervision. Moving from occasional hospital check-ups to continuous community-based monitoring requires a device small enough to be implanted or worn comfortably, yet capable of transmitting physiological data wirelessly over long periods on a small battery. This project addresses precisely that dual challenge: on the communication side, the MICS band at 402–405 MHz is the internationally designated frequency for medical implant wireless links because radio waves at this frequency travel well through human tissue, but designing an antenna that is both small enough for an implant and efficient enough to meet safety requirements is a difficult engineering problem that conventional approaches cannot solve without significant performance penalties. On the sensing side, recent progress in very low power electronics and on-device machine learning now makes it possible to acquire clinical-quality physiological signals and perform real-time health assessment directly on the wearable device itself, removing the need for continuous high-speed wireless transmission and allowing the device to communicate only when a medically relevant event is detected.


Theme 1: Metasurface Magnetoceramic Antenna Design for Body-Worn Implant Telemetry

Main Tasks:

  1. Characterise the electromagnetic properties of the magnetoceramic substrate material across the frequency range of interest, and use the measured parameters to build an accurate simulation model.
  2. Design and optimise the metasurface unit cell geometry and the complete antenna structure through full-wave electromagnetic simulation, targeting compact size, adequate bandwidth, and safe levels of energy absorption in body tissue.
  3. Fabricate the antenna prototype by patterning the metasurface array onto the magnetoceramic substrate, and prepare the necessary tissue-mimicking test environment for experimental validation.
  4. Measure and validate the antenna performance experimentally in terms of impedance matching, radiation characteristics, and tissue safety.
  5. Confirm the interface specification for integration with the sensor module developed in Theme 2 (if time permits).


Expected Outcomes:

  • A fabricated compact antenna prototype demonstrated to operate across the targeted medical implant and short-range wireless communication frequency bands
  • Experimental verification that the antenna meets accepted impedance matching, radiation efficiency, and body tissue safety standards
  • A comprehensive characterisation report comparing simulated and measured results, documenting the antenna's electromagnetic performance
  • A defined interface specification confirming the antenna is ready for integration with the sensor module developed in Theme 2


Theme 2: Wearable Cardiac Monitoring Sensor Module with On-Device AI Inference

Main Tasks:

  1. Design and validate the bio-signal acquisition circuit, selecting appropriate low-power components to capture the required physiological signals with sufficient quality and with effective rejection of electrical interference from the environment.
  2. Develop the embedded firmware on a suitable low-power wireless microcontroller, implementing multi-channel signal acquisition, a power management strategy to maximise battery life, and wireless transmission of data and alerts to an external receiver.
  3. Select, train, and deploy an on-device machine learning classifier capable of detecting cardiac arrhythmias in real time directly on the microcontroller, using a suitable publicly available labelled dataset for training and validation.
  4. Fabricate a compact prototype circuit board, validate its bio-signal acquisition performance against a clinical reference, conduct a small volunteer study to assess real-world classification accuracy.
  5. Integrate the completed module with the Theme 1 antenna (if time permits).


Expected Outcomes:

  • A fabricated compact wearable sensor module capable of acquiring multiple physiological signals continuously and simultaneously
  • Experimental verification that the acquired bio-signals meet clinically acceptable quality standards, validated against an appropriate reference instrument
  • An on-device arrhythmia classifier demonstrating satisfactory detection sensitivity and specificity, with inference speed and power consumption compatible with continuous wearable operation
  • A power consumption characterisation confirming that the complete module can sustain continuous monitoring over a clinically meaningful period on a small battery
  • A volunteer study report confirming real-world signal quality and classifier performance against a clinical reference

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background

Integrated Sensing and Communication, known as ISAC, is an emerging wireless technology concept in which radio signals are used for both communication and sensing. In future smart buildings, industrial facilities, healthcare spaces, and emergency-response environments, wireless systems may support data communication while also providing useful awareness of indoor environmental changes, movement, or occupancy-related behaviour. This project will investigate a civilian, educational, and laboratory-scale ISAC demonstrator for smart indoor sensing and wireless communication.

The project will be based only on open and public-domain material, including textbook-level wireless communication, OFDM principles, RF propagation, antenna concepts, channel measurement, and signal processing methods. The project will not involve surveillance, identification of individuals, military applications, espionage, security targeting, or any unpublished controlled technology.

Main Task

The main task is to design, implement, integrate, and evaluate a low-power ISAC demonstrator that combines a basic wireless communication function with a basic sensing function. The system will use a controlled laboratory setup where a transmitted RF signal is received and analysed for both communication quality and sensing-related changes. Depending on available laboratory resources, the project may use software-defined radio, low-cost RF modules, or simulation-supported hardware.

The communication part will evaluate basic link performance, such as received signal strength, signal-to-noise ratio, synchronization quality, channel response, and error behaviour. The sensing part will focus on simple controlled indoor scenarios, such as movement detection, object presence, or occupancy-related environmental changes, without identifying any individual. The project will quantify how communication and sensing performance are affected by distance, antenna position, multipath, movement, clutter, receiver noise, and measurement uncertainty.

The project addresses a complex engineering problem because ISAC requires trade-offs between waveform design, receiver synchronization, antenna and channel behaviour, sensing accuracy, communication reliability, and practical system integration. Students will need to make independent design choices, test their assumptions, evaluate uncertainty, and integrate their subsystem into a complete demonstrator.

Division of Labour

Student 1: ISAC Transmitter and Waveform Design

Student 1 will focus on the transmitter and waveform design part of the system. This student will review open-domain ISAC and OFDM principles, select or implement a suitable low-power communication waveform, define the signal frame structure, configure the signal generation chain, and evaluate transmitted signal parameters such as bandwidth, frequency, modulation, pilot symbols, and transmit power. The student will study how the transmitted waveform can support both communication and sensing functions. The expected output from this student is a documented ISAC signal generation block.

Student 2: Receiver Design, Synchronization, and Data Acquisition

Student 2 will focus on the receiver and data acquisition part of the system. This student will configure or design the receiver chain, study sampling rate, gain control, filtering, synchronization, channel estimation, dynamic range, and receiver noise level. The student will develop a repeatable data acquisition process and evaluate receiver performance using metrics such as received signal strength, signal-to-noise ratio, waveform quality, synchronization accuracy, and measurement repeatability. The expected output from this student is a documented receiver and communication performance evaluation block.

Student 3: Antenna, Channel, and Indoor Measurement Setup

Student 3 will focus on antenna selection or design, channel behaviour, and indoor measurement setup. This student will select or design suitable antennas, study antenna placement, polarization, antenna separation, and indoor multipath effects, and prepare controlled test scenarios for indoor sensing. The student will compare different measurement geometries and evaluate how the indoor channel affects both communication and sensing performance. The expected output from this student is a documented antenna and channel characterization block.

Student 4: Sensing Algorithm, Data Analysis, and Software Dashboard

Student 4 will focus on sensing signal processing, data analysis, and software visualization. This student will develop MATLAB or Python software for filtering, background subtraction, time-domain analysis, frequency-domain analysis, feature extraction, and simple movement or occupancy-related detection. Where appropriate, the student may compare classical signal processing methods with simple machine learning methods, but the project will not be limited to applying existing AI tools to a dataset. The student will also create a basic visualization dashboard showing communication metrics, sensing output, and detection confidence. The expected output from this student is a documented sensing algorithm and software interface block.

Common Integration Work

All four students will jointly define the system-level interface between transmitter, receiver, antenna/channel setup, and software processing. They will agree on shared parameters such as carrier frequency, bandwidth, waveform structure, sampling rate, antenna position, measurement distance, test scenarios, and data format. The final integrated system will demonstrate both a basic communication function and a basic sensing function under controlled laboratory conditions.

Expected Outcomes

The expected outcomes are:

  1. A low-power ISAC transmitter and waveform generation setup.
  2. A receiver, synchronization, and data acquisition setup.
  3. An antenna and indoor channel measurement setup.
  4. MATLAB or Python signal processing and sensing software.
  5. A basic software dashboard for communication and sensing visualization.
  6. A controlled experimental dataset collected in laboratory conditions.
  7. An integrated ISAC laboratory demonstrator.
  8. Performance evaluation including communication quality, sensing consistency, false alarm behaviour, signal-to-noise ratio, uncertainty analysis, and practical limitations.

1. Background

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, progressively destroying memory and cognition. Because structural brain changes precede severe symptoms, early and accurate detection from MRI offers a window for intervention, yet distinguishing neighbouring disease stages (non demented, very mild, mild, moderate) is difficult because adjacent classes share subtle features. This final year BSc engineering project develops a machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) pipeline for AD detection and multi stage classification from structural MRI, built entirely on established, publicly available research cohorts so the work is reproducible and ethically sound. The project is organised as one broad theme with four independent sub themes that share a common foundation: the same public cohorts (ADNI and OASIS, with AIBL as an external test set), a shared preprocessing pipeline (registration, skull stripping with tools such as FreeSurfer and FSL, intensity normalisation, and either 2D slice extraction or 3D volumes), a common four class staging scheme, and a unified evaluation protocol. This shared base allows the team to collaborate on the clinical understanding of AD progression, neuroimaging biomarkers, and the datasets, while each student owns a distinct methodological contribution and writes an independent thesis.


2. Main Task

Sub theme 1: Multi class AD staging with transfer learning

  • Preprocess ADNI and OASIS into a consistent four class staging dataset.
  • Compare pretrained feature extractors (ResNet152V2, VGG16, InceptionV3, MobileNet) and fusion architectures.
  • Handle severe class imbalance, particularly the scarcity of moderate dementia cases.

Sub theme 2: 3D and spatiotemporal deep learning

  • Build 3D volumetric inputs from the cohorts rather than single slices.
  • Implement 3D CNNs and combined 3D CNN plus transformer hybrids (such as video Swin style models).
  • Evaluate separation of AD from cognitively normal cases and of early from late MCI.

Sub theme 3: Cross cohort generalisation and robustness

  • Define training and external test splits across cohorts (for example ADNI to OASIS or AIBL).
  • Apply domain adaptation, harmonisation, and augmentation to reduce the multisite performance drop.
  • Run leave one site out evaluation to measure true generalisation.

Sub theme 4: Explainable AD detection (XAI)

  • Apply Grad-CAM, SHAP, and attention maps to the team's strongest models.
  • Localise the brain regions driving predictions (such as the hippocampus and ventricles).
  • Validate that the models attend to clinically meaningful atrophy rather than artefacts.


3. Expected Outcome

Sub theme 1

  • A reproducible four class staging pipeline with competitive accuracy.
  • A comparison of feature extractors and imbalance handling strategies.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Sub theme 2

  • Trained 3D and hybrid models exploiting full volumetric context.
  • Evidence on the benefit of volumetric over slice based analysis.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Sub theme 3

  • Quantified cross cohort performance and the effect of adaptation methods.
  • A practical recipe for improving robustness across scanners and sites.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Sub theme 4

  • Visual and quantitative explanations linking predictions to brain regions.
  • An assessment of clinical plausibility and trustworthiness.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

  • "Classification of Alzheimer's disease using advanced deep learning and ensemble techniques" (2025). Soft Computing (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00500-025-10953-w

1. Background

Brain tumours are among the most aggressive cancers, and accurate, early identification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is critical for treatment planning and patient survival. Manual reading of MRI is slow, subjective, and varies between radiologists, which motivates automated machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) support tools. This final year BSc engineering project investigates a complete ML pipeline for brain tumour analysis, covering detection, classification, delineation, and trustworthy decision support, built entirely on publicly available, anonymised MRI datasets so the work is fully reproducible and free of data access barriers. The project is organised as one broad theme with four independent sub themes that share a common foundation: the same public datasets (the Kaggle Brain Tumour MRI Dataset of glioma, meningioma, pituitary, and no tumour classes; the BraTS multimodal glioma collection with T1, contrast enhanced T1, T2, and FLAIR sequences; and the Figshare brain tumour set), a shared preprocessing convention (skull stripping, intensity normalisation, resizing, augmentation), and a common evaluation protocol. This shared base lets the team collaborate on understanding the clinical problem, the imaging modalities, and the datasets, while each student owns a methodologically distinct contribution and writes an independent thesis.


2. Main Task

Sub theme 1: Tumour classification with deep CNNs and transfer learning

  • Assemble and preprocess the combined public classification datasets into a balanced four class set.
  • Build and compare pretrained backbones (VGG16, ResNet152V2, EfficientNet, MobileNet) with fine tuning.
  • Study the effect of class imbalance and data augmentation on accuracy and generalisation.

Sub theme 2: Tumour segmentation on multimodal MRI

  • Prepare the BraTS multimodal volumes and tumour sub region labels (enhancing tumour, tumour core, edema).
  • Implement and train segmentation models (U-Net, nnU-Net, and a transformer based variant such as a Swin or ViT hybrid).
  • Evaluate boundary accuracy per sub region using Dice and Hausdorff distance.

Sub theme 3: Transformer and hybrid architectures for tumour recognition

  • Implement Vision Transformer and hybrid CNN plus transformer models for classification and detection.
  • Benchmark global context modelling against the pure CNN baseline from Sub theme 1 on identical splits.
  • Analyse the trade off between accuracy, model size, and training cost.

Sub theme 4: Explainable and robust diagnosis (XAI)

  • Apply interpretability methods (Grad-CAM, SHAP, attention and causal attribution maps) to the other sub themes' models.
  • Assess robustness across datasets and scanners through cross dataset testing.
  • Identify failure cases and quantify the trust and transparency gap.



3. Expected Outcome

Sub theme 1

  • A reproducible classification pipeline reaching competitive accuracy on the four class task.
  • A comparative study of backbones and augmentation strategies.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Sub theme 2

  • Trained segmentation models with per region Dice and Hausdorff results on BraTS.
  • A comparison of convolutional and transformer based segmentation.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Sub theme 3

  • A benchmarked transformer and hybrid model evaluated against the CNN baseline.
  • Evidence on when global context modelling helps tumour recognition.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Sub theme 4

  • Visual and quantitative explanations for the team's best models.
  • A robustness and generalisation analysis across datasets and scanners.
  • An independent thesis and a candidate conference paper.

Engineering Resilient and Inclusive Smart Infrastructure for Future Communities


Modern communities face increasingly complex engineering challenges arising from ageing infrastructure, climate change, demographic shifts, digital transformation, and growing demands for equitable access to services. These challenges are characterised by uncertainty, conflicting stakeholder priorities, and the absence of single optimal solutions. Recent literature highlights the importance of systems engineering, human-centred design, sustainability, and interdisciplinary innovation in addressing such problems. This theme project aims to design an integrated suite of engineering solutions that enhance the resilience, inclusivity, and sustainability of future communities. Students will apply engineering and creativity to develop technically rigorous solutions while considering health and safety, regulatory compliance, diversity and inclusion, environmental impact, commercial viability, and user acceptance. Collectively, the projects will contribute to a digital twin of a future community, enabling evaluation of trade-offs between performance, cost, societal benefit, and sustainability before implementation.


Project 1. Intelligent Urban Flood Prediction and Early Warning System


Key Tasks: Timely prediction of urban flooding is essential for reducing damage to infrastructure and protecting communities. Advances in IoT sensing, weather forecasting, and machine learning have enabled the development of real-time flood prediction systems capable of providing actionable warnings despite uncertainties in environmental conditions.


Expected Outcomes: Students will produce a flood forecasting framework capable of predicting flood events with quantified uncertainty. Deliverables may include predictive algorithms, simulation results, performance evaluation under different weather scenarios, and recommendations for practical deployment in smart cities.


References


Flood prediction using machine learning models: Literature review https://doi.org/10.3390/w10111536


Exploring the use of Artificial Intelligence for flood forecasting in Scotland https://www.crew.ac.uk/sites/www.crew.ac.uk/files/publication/CSPF2025_01_Main_Report_Final_2025_08_06.pdf


A critical review of real-time modelling of flood forecasting in urban drainage systems https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.127476


Ai-driven approaches to flood risk management: overcoming data bias and enhancing decision-making https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crm.2025.100752.


Project 2: Adaptive Drainage Infrastructure Control Using Predictive Optimisation


Key tasks: Traditional drainage systems typically operate using fixed rules and are often unable to adapt to rapidly changing weather conditions. Real-time control strategies can dynamically optimise the operation of pumps, gates, and retention facilities to minimise flooding while balancing energy use and operational constraints.


Expected Outcomes: Students will deliver an adaptive control strategy demonstrating improved flood resilience compared with conventional rule-based operation. Outputs may include optimisation models, digital simulations, resilience analyses, and engineering recommendations for implementation.


References


Modeling and real-time control of urban drainage systems: A review https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2015.08.007


Model predictive control of urban drainage systems: A review and perspective towards smart real-time water management https://doi.org/10.1080/10643389.2018.1455484


Project 3: Resilient Energy Management System for Critical Community Facilities


Key Tasks: Design a simulation model of a community microgrid supplying critical facilities such as hospitals, emergency shelters, and water treatment units. The system should optimise distributed renewable generation, battery storage dispatch, and demand-side load prioritisation under normal and grid-disturbance conditions.


Expected Outcomes: Students will demonstrate improved energy reliability and operational resilience by comparing baseline and optimised control strategies under outage and peak-demand scenarios.


References


From flexible building to resilient energy communities: A scalable decentralized energy management scheme based on collaborative agent https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2025.115651


How to build resilient community energy systems? Lessons from Malawi and Ethiopia https://doi.org/10.1088/2634-4505/adb0eb


Community Energy and Community Resilience: A Multi-Dimensional Perspective https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-57938-7_2


Project 4: AI-Based Load Forecasting and Adaptive Grid Control for Microgrid Stability


Key Tasks: Develop a simulation framework for a community microgrid that integrates short-term load forecasting using AI techniques and adaptive control of energy resources. The model should evaluate how predictive control strategies improve decision-making for storage usage, renewable integration, and emergency load shedding under uncertain demand and supply conditions.


Expected Outcomes: Students will demonstrate enhanced grid stability, reduced energy wastage, and improved cost-efficiency through predictive simulation and scenario-based optimisation.


References


Artificial intelligence-driven smart grid optimization: A comprehensive review of machine learning, renewable integration, and cybersecurity applications https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecmx.2026.101849


Hybrid deep learning based load forecasting and AI-driven energy management for grid-connected multi-microgrids https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compeleceng.2025.110915


Real-Time Load Forecasting and Adaptive Control in Smart Grids Using a Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy Approach https://doi.org/10.3390/en17112539


Project 5: Simulation of Wearable Sensor-Based Indoor Navigation for Visually Impaired Users


Key Tasks: Develop a simulation environment for an indoor assistive navigation system that integrates wearable sensors (e.g., cameras, IMUs, or LiDAR-based devices) with environmental mapping and localisation algorithms. The system should model real-time obstacle detection, path planning, and feedback delivery (audio/haptic), while considering user movement uncertainty and indoor layout complexity.


Expected Outcomes: A validated simulation demonstrating improved navigation accuracy, reduced collision risk, and enhanced route efficiency for visually impaired users compared to baseline non-adaptive navigation strategies.


References


A comprehensive review of navigation systems for visually impaired individuals https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e31825


A Wearable Navigation Device for Visually Impaired People Based on the Real-Time Semantic Visual SLAM System https://doi.org/10.3390/s21041536


RGB-D camera based wearable navigation system for the visually impaired  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cviu.2016.03.019


Project 6: AI-Driven Indoor Mobility Digital Twin for Visually Impaired Navigation Support


Key Tasks: Develop a digital twin of a complex indoor environment (e.g., hospital, shopping centre, or university building) to simulate navigation for visually impaired users. The system should integrate spatial mapping, agent-based user modelling, and AI-driven path planning to evaluate different assistive strategies such as audio cues, haptic guidance, and dynamic obstacle prediction. The simulation should also model uncertainty in perception, walking speed variability, and environmental changes (e.g., moving crowds or temporary obstructions).


Expected Outcomes: A validated simulation framework demonstrating improved navigation efficiency, reduced collision probability, and enhanced accessibility through adaptive guidance strategies in dynamic indoor environments.


References


Designing Human-Centred Adaptive AI Navigation for Blind and Visually Impaired Individuals: A Cognitive Load-Aware Framework for Accessible Urban Mobility https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7060206


From synthetic navigation data to real-world mobility cues: Reinforcement learning for sensory substitution in visual impairment https://doi.org/10.1016/j.array.2026.100861


Project 7: Development of a Simulation-Based Digital Twin for Civil Infrastructure Systems


Key Tasks: Develop a high-fidelity digital twin model of a selected civil infrastructure asset such as a bridge, tunnel, or elevated roadway. Students will integrate geometric modelling, material properties, and environmental loading conditions into a simulation environment capable of representing structural behaviour under operational stresses. The model should be designed to interface with external data inputs such as sensor readings or inspection outputs from autonomous robots.


Expected Outcome: Students will produce a validated digital twin simulation platform capable of replicating realistic structural response under variable loading and environmental conditions. The outcome will include a configurable simulation environment ready for integration with inspection and monitoring systems.


References


Literature review of digital twin technologies for civil infrastructure https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iintel.2023.100050


Development of Digital Twin for Intelligent Maintenance of Civil Infrastructure https://doi.org/10.3390/su14148664


Digital Twin: Mitigating Unpredictable, Undesirable Emergent Behavior in Complex Systems https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-38756-7_4


Digital Twin: Enabling Technologies, Challenges and Open Research https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2020.2998358


Project 8: Probabilistic Structural Health Prognostics and Risk-Informed Maintenance Planning for Civil Infrastructure


Key Tasks: Develop a simulation-based framework to estimate structural degradation and predict remaining useful life (RUL) of infrastructure assets without relying on a full digital twin model. Students will use probabilistic modelling, statistical learning, or physics-informed degradation models to simulate deterioration processes such as fatigue cracking, corrosion growth, or joint weakening under variable loading and environmental conditions. The system must explicitly account for uncertainty in inspection data, material variability, and operational loading scenarios. Students will also design a risk-based maintenance decision model that prioritises interventions based on safety criticality, service disruption impact, and lifecycle cost optimisation. The model should be tested across multiple simulated infrastructure scenarios to evaluate robustness and reliability.


Expected Outcome: Students will produce a predictive maintenance and risk assessment framework capable of estimating infrastructure degradation and optimising inspection and repair schedules under uncertainty. The outcome will include simulation results demonstrating improved safety-risk management and cost efficiency compared to rule-based maintenance strategies.


References

Molecular communication (MC) is an emerging interdisciplinary field that studies the transmission, propagation, and reception of information using chemical molecules, inspired by communication mechanisms naturally occurring in biological systems [1]. MC has significant potential in applications where conventional electromagnetic communications are unsuitable, including targeted drug delivery, biosensing, environmental monitoring, synthetic biology, and Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) systems.


Chemical reaction networks integrated with microfluidic systems provide a promising platform for performing computation and signal processing directly in the molecular domain. Inspired by digital electronic circuits, chemical computing systems can implement arithmetic operations, logic functions, and information processing using molecular transport and chemical reactions [2]. This theme focuses on the design, simulation, and analysis of microfluidic circuits capable of performing information processing tasks using chemical reactions. Students will explore how computation can be realized without electronics, using only molecules, reactions, and microfluidic structures.


Project 1 Design, Simulation, and Analysis of Chemical Logic Gates in Microfluidic Systems

This project focuses on reproducing and evaluating chemical-reaction-based logic gates implemented in microfluidic environments [3]. The student will study how fundamental digital logic operations can be realized using molecular transport and chemical reactions. The student will:

  • Review the fundamentals of chemical computing and molecular communication.
  • Study the five-layer microfluidic architecture proposed for chemical signal processing.
  • Implement simulation models of microfluidic logic gates, including AND, OR, NAND, NOR, and XOR gates.
  • Investigate the role of diffusion, convection, reaction kinetics, and channel geometry in logic-gate operation.
  • Evaluate logic correctness, signal delay, and robustness under different operating conditions.


Project 2: Design, Simulation, and Analysis of an End-to-End Molecular Communication System

This project focuses on reproducing a published chemical-reaction-based microfluidic molecular communication system consisting of a transmitter, propagation channel, and receiver [4]. The student will investigate how information can be encoded, transmitted, and decoded using chemical reactions in a microfluidic environment. The student will:

  • Review the fundamentals of molecular communication systems.
  • Study the design of chemical-reaction-based microfluidic transmitters and receivers.
  • Develop simulation models of the end-to-end molecular communication system using Smoldyn.
  • Simulate the transmission of binary information using concentration-based signaling.
  • Investigate the effects of channel length, flow rate, diffusion coefficient, and reaction parameters on system behavior.
  • Evaluate communication performance in terms of channel response, signal distortion, delay, and bit error rate (BER).


Addressing FYP Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs): These projects provide students with opportunities to undertake independent project planning and execution, conduct literature reviews, apply mathematical and engineering principles, critically evaluate technical outcomes, assess broader societal and environmental impacts, demonstrate professional and ethical practice, and develop technical report writing and oral presentation skills.


 

[1] Bi, D., Almpanis, A., Noel, A., Deng, Y. and Schober, R., 2021. A survey of molecular communication in cell biology: Establishing a new hierarchy for interdisciplinary applications. IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, 23(3), pp.1494-1545.

[2] Walter, V., Bi, D., Salehi-Reyhani, A. and Deng, Y., 2023. Real-time signal processing via chemical reactions for a microfluidic molecular communication system. Nature Communications, 14(1), p.7188.

[3] Lotter, S., Brand, L., Jamali, V., Schäfer, M., Loos, H.M., Unterweger, H., Greiner, S., Kirchner, J., Alexiou, C., Drummer, D. and Fischer, G., 2023. Experimental research in synthetic molecular communications–Part I. IEEE Nanotechnology Magazine, 17(3), pp.42-53.

[4] Bi, D., Deng, Y., Pierobon, M. and Nallanathan, A., 2020. Chemical reactions-based microfluidic transmitter and receiver design for molecular communication. IEEE Transactions on Communications, 68(9), pp.5590-5605.

1. Background

Precision agriculture leverages IoT technologies to monitor environmental conditions and optimise farming practices. With the growing demand for sustainable food production, data-driven techniques can help farmers make timely and resource-efficient decisions. This theme project brings together four students to design an end-to-end precision agriculture system that integrates environmental sensing, automation, plant/pest monitoring, and cloud-based analytics.

The work is organised as a single coherent theme, but each student owns an independent design problem with its own literature review, design, implementation, and testing. The subsystems communicate through a shared, agreed interface so that the individual contributions combine into one working prototype, while each remains assessable as a stand-alone engineering design. The system is intended for civilian, small-scale farm use only and is built entirely from published, open-domain techniques and components.

2. Main Task

Develop and prototype a modular IoT system for a small-scale farm setup. The system consists of distributed sensing and monitoring nodes, an automated irrigation controller, a communication backbone, and a combined data platform that provides visualisation, alerting, and recommendations. The team will simulate or implement field conditions and test the system's effectiveness in monitoring and optimising crop management. Each of the four students delivers one subsystem and demonstrates how it meets a defined combination of user, environmental, and operational needs, including reliability, power, cost, and safety in an outdoor farm context.

3. Expected Outcomes

• Distributed sensing covering soil and weather conditions.

• Camera/sensor-based monitoring of plant health and pest presence.

• Automated, sensor-driven irrigation control.

• A combined data platform: ingestion, storage, live dashboard, alerting, and recommendations.

• Documentation, test results, and recommendations based on field simulation or lab testing.

4. Individual Work Directions and Objectives

The original concept has been consolidated into four independent student roles. The soil and weather units are combined into a single Environmental Sensing Node; the crop-imaging and pest-detection units are combined into a single Crop Health & Pest Monitoring Node; and the dashboard and analytics functions are combined into a single Data Platform owning the full backbone from ingestion through to recommendations. Each role below is a distinct design problem with minimal overlap.


Student 1 — Environmental Sensing Node (Soil & Weather)

Literature Review: Study soil moisture and temperature sensing techniques together with low-cost weather station designs, and their combined relevance to irrigation and crop planning.

System Design: Select suitable sensors for soil moisture, soil temperature, rainfall, light, humidity, and air temperature, and integrate them with a single microcontroller-based node, addressing weatherproofing and power.

Implementation: Build a node that collects soil and weather data and transmits it wirelessly to the data platform at set intervals.

Testing: Evaluate sensor accuracy across varying soil and weather conditions (wet/dry, temperature range) and validate weather readings against reference datasets or calibrated instruments.


Student 2 — Smart Irrigation Controller

Literature Review: Explore irrigation scheduling techniques and sensor-based automation strategies.

System Design: Develop control logic that uses incoming soil and weather data to decide when to activate irrigation valves, defining clear, safe actuation rules.

Implementation: Create a controller that interfaces with solenoids or pumps and acts on data received from the sensing node and commands from the platform.

Testing: Simulate different soil-moisture scenarios and verify that irrigation behaviour responds correctly and safely.


Student 3 — Crop Health & Pest Monitoring Node

Literature Review: Investigate imaging methods for plant health monitoring and IoT-based pest detection methods, comparing camera-based and sensor-based approaches.

System Design: Use an embedded camera (and, where suitable, a light trap with sensors) to capture periodic images and detect signs of plant stress and insect presence.

Implementation: Implement image- or signal-based analysis to flag unhealthy plants and classify pest presence, and report results to the data platform.

Testing: Compare outputs across healthy versus stressed plant setups and simulated or lab-captured pest specimens to assess detection reliability.


Student 4 — Data Platform: Integration, Monitoring & Analytics

Literature Review: Study dashboard UX/UI approaches and suitable frameworks (e.g., Node-RED, Flask); data ingestion and time-series storage for heterogeneous sensor streams; methods for handling input-data uncertainty; and simple, interpretable data-analysis/ML approaches in farming (e.g., regression, threshold-based rules).

System Design: Design a pub/sub ingestion layer (e.g., MQTT) with a defined API that all nodes publish to, plus time-series storage; a live dashboard with charts, alerts (using hysteresis/debouncing to avoid alert storms) and remote access; offline-first store-and-forward for poor rural connectivity; a command path to the irrigation controller with acknowledgement and failure handling; and recommendation logic that converts combined data into irrigation, fertilisation, or pest-control guidance. Remote access uses standard published mechanisms (TLS, token-based auth) — applying established practice, not developing new encryption.

Implementation: Build the ingestion layer, storage, dashboard interface, alerting, and a rule-based or predictive recommendation engine as one integrated platform serving the three field subsystems.

Testing: Measure real-time update latency; test behaviour under missing, late, out-of-order, and conflicting readings and simulated node dropouts; assess performance as node count scales; and compare the system's recommendations against known optimal actions on simulated datasets.


5. Integration and Independence

To satisfy the requirement that each project be independent with minimal overlap, the four students agree a shared data and communication interface early in the project but design and build their own subsystems separately. The three field subsystems (Students 1-3) each design against that interface, while Student 4 owns the platform that receives, stores, presents, and acts on their data. Each subsystem can be tested in isolation against the agreed interface, and the team integrates them into a single demonstrable prototype for the final defence. This lets every student evidence their own design decisions, analysis of input-data uncertainty, and consideration of the wider engineering context, while the combined system shows the full precision-agriculture workflow from sensing through to recommendation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Molecular communication (MC) is an emerging interdisciplinary field that studies the transmission, propagation, and reception of information using chemical molecules, inspired by communication mechanisms naturally occurring in biological systems [1]. MC has significant potential in applications where conventional electromagnetic communications are unsuitable, including targeted drug delivery, biosensing, environmental monitoring, synthetic biology, and Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) systems.

 

Over the past decade, extensive theoretical research has been conducted to understand molecular propagation channels and communication mechanisms. However, experimental validation remains a key challenge [2], [3]. Developing practical MC platforms is essential for validating theoretical models, investigating real-world communication constraints, and enabling future MC-enabled applications.

 

This project theme focuses on the design, implementation, and evaluation of experimental molecular communication systems operating in either air or liquid environments. Students will gain hands-on experience in system design, sensing technologies, embedded systems, signal processing, data analysis, and mathematical modelling. All projects under this theme require students to:

  • Conduct a literature review on molecular communication systems and relevant sensing technologies.
  • Design and implement an experimental communication platform consisting of transmitter and receiver components.
  • Select suitable signaling molecules and modulation schemes.
  • Develop software and hardware for signal generation, acquisition, and processing.
  • Evaluate system performance using communication metrics such as bit error rate (BER), delay, reliability, and data rate.
  • Analyze experimental results and compare them with theoretical expectations.
  • Consider practical constraints including safety, scalability, energy efficiency, and application requirements.

 

Project 1 Air-Based Molecular Communication System Design and Performance Analysis

This project focuses on molecular communication through gaseous media [4]. The student will design and construct an air-based MC testbed capable of controlled chemical release and molecular detection. The student will:

  • Select suitable signaling molecules and gas sensors.
  • Design and implement transmitter and receiver hardware.
  • Develop communication protocols and modulation methods.
  • Evaluate system performance in terms of BER, data rate, delay, and communication range.
  • Develop mathematical models to characterise molecule propagation and system behavior.

 

Project 2: Robotic Chemical Source Tracking Using Air-Based Molecular Communication

This project extends air-based MC systems to mobile sensing applications [5]. The student will design and implement an air-based molecular communication receiver mounted on a mobile robotic platform capable of locating a chemical source. The student will:

  • Design an air-based molecular communication transmitter and receiver.
  • Integrate chemical sensing hardware with a mobile robot.
  • Develop source localization and tracking algorithms.
  • Investigate how environmental factors influence tracking performance.
  • Evaluate localisation accuracy, response time, and robustness under different operating conditions.

Potential applications include environmental monitoring, hazardous gas detection, and autonomous inspection systems.


Project 3 Liquid-Based Molecular Communication System Design and Performance Analysis

This project investigates molecular communication in liquid environments, which are particularly relevant to biomedical and microfluidic applications [6]. The student will:

  • Design and construct a liquid-based molecular communication platform.
  • Implement controlled molecular release and detection mechanisms.
  • Select suitable signaling molecules and sensing technologies.
  • Measure communication performance including BER, delay, throughput, and channel response.
  • Develop mathematical models to characterize molecular transport and communication performance.

Potential applications include lab-on-a-chip systems, biosensing, and targeted drug delivery.


Project 4 Multi-Molecule Detection for Liquid-Based Molecular Communication Systems

This project explores advanced modulation schemes for liquid-based molecular communication using multiple molecule types. Unlike conventional concentration-based signaling, information will be encoded using different molecular species [7]. The student will: 

  • Design and implement a liquid-based molecular communication platform.
  • Select two distinguishable signaling molecules to represent binary information.
  • Develop sensing and signal-processing methods capable of differentiating molecule types.
  • Design decoding algorithms for molecular classification and detection.
  • Evaluate communication performance and compare it with conventional single-molecule approaches.

The project provides opportunities to investigate novel molecular modulation and detection techniques for future high-capacity MC systems.

 

Addressing FYP Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs): These projects provide students with opportunities to undertake independent project planning and execution, conduct literature reviews, apply mathematical and engineering principles, critically evaluate technical outcomes, assess broader societal and environmental impacts, demonstrate professional and ethical practice, and develop technical report writing and oral presentation skills.

[2] Lotter, S., Brand, L., Jamali, V., Schäfer, M., Loos, H.M., Unterweger, H., Greiner, S., Kirchner, J., Alexiou, C., Drummer, D. and Fischer, G., 2023. Experimental research in synthetic molecular communications–Part I. IEEE Nanotechnology Magazine, 17(3), pp.42-53.

Theme Title: Compositional Normalization and Technical Dropout Deconvolution in Next-Generation Sequencing Pipelines

Next-generation sequencing instruments impose an arbitrary upper limit on the total number of reads generated per sample, making the resulting data inherently compositional. Because an increase in one taxon artificially forces the relative abundance of others to decrease, standard statistical metrics yield spurious correlations. This issue is compounded by extreme data sparsity, leaving engineers to determine whether a zero in a data matrix represents a true biological absence or a technical dropout caused by insufficient sequencing depth. To build reliable analysis pipelines, engineering teams must develop advanced computational blocks that apply compositional data analysis principles alongside probabilistic models capable of separating true low-abundance resident microbes from environmental, kit, and batch-effect contaminants.


Subproject 1. Benchmarking Variance-Stabilized vs Shrinkage-Log Transformation for Outlier-Resistant Feature Selection


In high-throughput count datasets (such as RNA-seq and metagenomics), naive variance filtering is severely confounded by mean-variance dependence and extreme sampling noise. This project evaluates the comparative performance of two robust, transformation-specific filtering frameworks: Median Absolute Deviation applied after Variance Stabilising Transformation and Median Absolute Deviation following a Regularised Logarithm Transformation.

Students will use empirical Bayes shrinkage and size-factor normalization to map highly overdispersed raw counts onto a homoskedastic, constant-variance scale, and apply it on a real microbiome dataset. By using MAD instead of standard deviation , the project will demonstrate how to isolate genuine biological variability from low-count artifacts and single-sample outliers.


Subproject 2. A Hybrid Framework for Sparse Microbiome Profiles: Combining Abundance, Zero Proportion, and Gini Index Filters


High sparsity, zero-inflation, and severe population inequality present massive challenges when analyzing microbial communities. This project aims to design an ensemble preprocessing pipeline that targets these artifacts sequentially. The pipeline combines an abundance-based Prevalence Filter (discarding rare features appearing below a sample fraction threshold π) with a Zero Proportion Filter to handle technical dropouts. Finally, a Gini Coefficient Filter is deployed to measure distribution inequality across samples , mapping sorted ascending count vectors against a rank index to weed out highly skewed features dominated by only a few samples. The performance will be optimized to maximize downstream statistical power and ordination stability, and will be applied to a real microbiome dataset..


Subproject 3. Advanced Modeling of Overdispersed Count Data: Comparing Dispersion Filters and Model-Based ZINB AIC


Count datasets typically violate Poisson assumptions because biological and technical variation lead to distinct overdispersion (σ2>μ). This project investigates the trade-offs between heuristic overdispersion metrics and explicit probabilistic modeling. First, students will implement a mathematical Dispersion Filter derived from the variance-mean relationship to retain features with non-random variation. Second, they will use a model-based filter using a Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial framework. By fitting parameters to each feature's count vector via the zinbwave package, the project will use the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to selectively retain features that exhibit highly structured, reliable model fits while excluding infinite-AIC or poorly fitted noise. To test these approaches, a real microbiome datasest will be provided.


Subproject 4: Uncovering Dynamic Biomarkers: Temporal Autocorrelation and Shannon Entropy Filters for Longitudinal Studies


Time-series perturbation experiments require filtering techniques that capture structured longitudinal dynamics rather than stationary noise. This project focuses on identifying dynamic biomarkers by combining a Time Correlation Filter with a Temporal Autocorrelation Filter and a Shannon Entropy Filter. Students will compute Pearson correlation coefficients against continuous time vectors alongside lag-ℓ autocorrelation coefficients to catch underlying rhythmicity, delay-response patterns, or circadian trends. This temporal analysis is paired with Shannon entropy calculations on normalized sample probability distributions to robustly filter out flat, uniform distributions or uninformative zero-inflated signals , isolating highly informative, dynamically fluctuating biological features. To test these approaches, a real microbiome dataset will be provided.

Theme Title: Multi-Omics Fusion Frameworks for High-Dimensional Microbiome Feature Spaces

The primary computational challenge in modern microbiome research stems from the structural asymmetry of data types. Current studies generate an array of disparate data layers, including compositional amplicon reads, deep metagenomic shotgun sequences, and continuous mass spectrometry peaks from metabolomics. Integrating these inputs creates an extreme high-dimensional statistical environment where the number of parameters vastly outnumbers the biological replicates. This data heterogeneity increases the risk of model overfitting and false discoveries. Resolving this requires the engineering of robust machine learning architectures capable of aligning these distinct data structures into unified, predictive latent spaces without sacrificing the unique statistical properties of each underlying biological layer.


Subproject 1. Unsupervised Latent Factor Dissection and Cross-Omic Sample Stratification Using MOFA2 and SNF


This project focuses on the unsupervised integration of highly heterogeneous multi-omic cohorts (such as matching metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and metabolomic profiles) to uncover hidden disease subtypes. Students will implement Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA2) to decompose the broad variance of the coupled datasets into orthogonal latent factors, pinpointing which omic modalities drive specific clinical variations. In parallel, Similarity Network Fusion (SNF) will be utilized to construct distinct sample-similarity networks for each layer, which are fused using a non-linear iterative process to preserve both common and complementary signals. The project will benchmark the sample stratification achieved by the fused SNF network against the low-dimensional embeddings generated by MOFA2, assessing their stability and biological interpretation. To test these approaches, real microbiome dataset will be provided.


Subproject 2. Supervised Multi-Group Biomarker Discovery and Robust Validation via DIABLO and RGCCA


Aimed at identifying discrete multi-omic signatures that characterize categorical phenotypes or treatment groups, this project evaluates supervised block-structured integration techniques. Students will design a predictive pipeline utilizing DIABLO (Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker discovery using Latent variable approaches for Omics), tuning the sparse penalty parameters to select minimal, highly correlated subsets of features across different data blocks that maximize group separation. To validate the robustness of these signatures against over-fitting and collinearity, Regularised Generalized Canonical Correlation Analysis (RGCCA) will be implemented as an independent statistical engine. By incorporating bootstrap resampling, students will calculate confidence intervals for the structural loadings, isolating reproducible cross-omic biomarkers. To test these approaches, real microbiome dataset will be provided.


Subproject 3. Mapping Context-Specific Metabolic Rewiring in Environmental Systems via IntLIM Nonlinear Modeling


Subproject 3. Rather than treating multi-omic relationships as static, this project models how molecular interactions dynamically alter across different environmental or clinical contexts (e.g., healthy versus perturbed states). Students will deploy Interaction Linear Modeling (IntLIM) to systematically evaluate pairs of continuous features, such as microbial abundances and downstream metabolite concentrations. By embedding a critical interaction term (Microbe×Phenotype) into the linear framework, the model will capture statistically significant changes in correlation slopes across distinct groups. The project will isolate instances of "mechanistic rewiring," highlighting specific pathways that are actively suppressed or upregulated by the underlying phenotypic state. To test these approaches, real microbiome dataset will be provided.


Subproject 4. Multi-Block Topological Network Inference and Synergistic Driver Identification


This project leverages the mathematical synergy between network theory and multi-block dimension reduction to construct comprehensive multi-omic interactomes. Students will combine the output of DIABLO’s cross-block correlation matrices and SNF’s fused similarity graphs to infer a unified, multi-layered topological network. By computing graph-theoretical metrics—such as betweenness centrality, degree distribution, and closeness centrality—the project will identify key "hub" features and bottleneck nodes that bridge disparate molecular layers (e.g., linking specific structural genes to metabolic endpoints). The final pipeline will deliver automated, publication-quality multi-omic network visualizations to elucidate the cascading biological mechanisms driving the ecosystem. To test these approaches, real microbiome dataset will be provided.

Simultaneous Multi-Wavelength Mode-Locked DFB Laser


1.      Background


Multi-wavelength mode-locked semiconductor lasers are essential for next-generation dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) communications, coherent LiDAR, and high-resolution photonic sensing. Existing implementations often require multiple discrete single-wavelength lasers and complex integration schemes, leading to increased footprint, power consumption, and manufacturing cost. This project seeks to develop a compact, monolithically integrated multi-wavelength mode-locked laser leveraging waveguide Bragg gratings (WBGs) or four-phase-shifted chirped-sampled Bragg gratings (4PS-CSBGs). By generating multiple phase-locked wavelengths from a single chip, the proposed device will deliver enhanced stability, scalability, and manufacturability, paving the way for highly integrated photonic systems.


2. Main Tasks


  • Simulate the material and modal gain of a five-quantum-well epilayer using Photonic Integrated Circuit (PIC)group MATLAB codes.
  • Simulate near-field and far-field patterns using RSoft BeamPROP software.
  • Design a WBG microcavity or 4PS-CSBG laser supporting triple- and six-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm using PIC group MATLAB codes.
  • Simulate device behaviour (transmission spectrum, group delay, and photon density profile) using the Transfer Matrix Method (TMM) with PIC group tools.
  • Design the fabrication process and characterisation setup, including:
  • Optical spectral measurements (Optical spectrum analyser),
  • Pulse width measurements (autocorrelator),
  • Radio frequency (RF) stability characterisation (Electrical spectrum analyser).


3. Expected Outcomes


  • Demonstrate four types of multi-wavelength mode-locked DFB lasers with stable wavelengths within a single cavity and a consistent free spectral range (FSR) across a wide range of DFB currents and saturable absorber (SA) reverse voltages.
  • Achieve nearly transform-limited pulses with a time-bandwidth product approaching the Fourier transform limit.
  • Quantify the performance variations associated with cavity length and π-phase shifts.


4. Student Work Distribution


  • Student 1: Design of the laser cavity and WBG structure for triple-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.
  • Student 2: Design of the laser cavity and WBG structure for six-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.
  • Student 3: Design of the laser cavity and 4PS-CSBG structure for triple-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.
  • Student 4: Design of the laser cavity and 4PS-CSBG structure for six-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.

Reconfigurable Multi-Passband Microwave Photonic Filters


1.      Background


Microwave signal filtering is essential in RF systems. Leveraging integrated photonics, emerging microwave photonic filter (PF) platforms offer reconfigurable, widely tunable filtering with advantages in size, weight, stability, power efficiency, and latency—beyond

what conventional electronics can achieve. This project develops a compact, monolithically integrated filter using thermally-tuned conventional or four-phase-shift sampled Bragg gratings (C-SBG or 4PS-SBG) on the Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) platform. Through the Reconstruction Equivalent Chirp (REC) technique, the design enables channel independence, wide tunability, low insertion loss, high side-mode suppression ratio (SMSR), and fine spectral resolution.


2. Main Tasks


· Use Lumerical FDE to simulate material properties, waveguide dimensions, effective refractive index (nₑff), and optical confinement of on-chip ridge waveguides.


· Analyse electric field distributions for single- and multi-mode operations and identify critical conditions using Lumerical FDE.


· Design C-band dual- and four-passband PFs based on equivalent chirped C-SBG or 4PS-SBG structures.


· Simulate static performance (transmission spectra, photon distribution) using Lumerical FDTD and the Transfer Matrix Method (TMM).


· Model dynamic behaviour (neff, phase shift, spectral tuning vs. temperature) with Lumerical FDE, FDTD, COMSOL Multiphysics, and TMM.


· Develop the fabrication process flow and experimental characterisation setup.


3. Expected Outcomes


· Demonstrate four multi-channel PFs with tunable passbands, adjustable spacing, and a broad stopband range.


· Achieve SMSR > 10 dB.


· Ensure -3 dB bandwidth of all filtering windows < 20 GHz.


· Quantify static spectrum variations based on phase shift magnitude, number, and position.


4. Student Work Distribution


· Student 1: Design and Optimisation of a Dual-Channel Filter Cavity with Equivalent-Chirp C-SBG at 1.55 μm


· Student 2: Design and Optimisation of a Dual-Channel Filter Cavity with Equivalent-Chirp 4PS-SBG at 1.55 μm


· Student 3: Design and Optimisation of a Quad-Channel Filter Cavity with Equivalent-Chirp C-SBG at 1.55 μm


·  Student 4: Design and Optimisation of a Quad-Channel Filter Cavity with Equivalent-Chirp 4PS-SBG at 1.55 μm

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System has become a major enabling technology for positioning, navigation, timing, and intelligent applications in China and beyond. In recent years, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, unmanned systems, and infrastructure inspection have all created increasing demand for high-accuracy and high-reliability positioning solutions. In Hainan, this demand is particularly relevant due to the development of coastal transportation, island logistics, low-altitude UAV applications, and digital infrastructure management.

However, standalone BeiDou positioning performance may degrade in practical scenarios due to signal blockage, multipath, limited satellite visibility, atmospheric disturbances, and temporary interruptions. For intelligent inspection tasks using drones or mobile platforms, positioning continuity is as important as positioning accuracy. Integrating BeiDou with an inertial navigation system (INS) is a practical and widely adopted solution, where inertial sensing provides short-term continuity and GNSS provides long-term correction.

2. Main Task

This project aims to develop a BeiDou/INS integrated positioning method for low-altitude intelligent inspection applications. The student will first study the principles of BeiDou positioning, inertial sensor errors, coordinate systems, motion modeling, and data fusion algorithms. The project may use public GNSS/IMU datasets, simulation data, or small-scale experimental datadepending on resource availability.

The main technical work is to implement and evaluate a fusion algorithm based on Kalman Filter, Extended Kalman Filter, Unscented Kalman Filter, or equivalent sensor fusion schemes. The system should estimate position, velocity, and possibly attitude information, and compare the performance of standalone BeiDou, standalone INS dead reckoning, and integrated BeiDou/INS solutions. The student is encouraged to consider realistic scenarios such as partial signal blockage or short GNSS outages of 5–20 seconds.

Quantitative objectives may include reducing positioning error by at least 30% compared with standalone BeiDou under degraded signal conditions, maintaining continuous trajectory output during simulated outages, and achieving stable trajectory reconstruction in representative inspection scenarios.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a BeiDou/INS positioning algorithm, a simulation or experimental evaluation platform, and a quantitative comparison of different positioning strategies. The final system should demonstrate improved accuracy, continuity, and robustness in low-altitude or mobile inspection scenarios. The dissertation should include theoretical modeling, algorithm implementation, trajectory analysis, and error statistics under multiple test conditions. This project is especially suitable for students interested in navigation, intelligent systems, low-altitude applications, and BeiDou-enabled engineering innovation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Communication and navigation systems increasingly operate in dense and complex electromagnetic environments, where different forms of intentional or unintentional interference may significantly degrade system reliability and service quality. In wireless communication systems, interference may reduce throughput and increase bit error rate; in navigation systems, especially satellite-based systems such as BeiDou, interference may cause signal loss, tracking failure, or severe positioning degradation. Therefore, accurate recognition of interference types is an important prerequisite for adaptive anti-jamming and interference mitigation.

Traditional interference recognition methods typically rely on manually designed features derived from the spectrum, energy distribution, bandwidth, or statistical properties of the received signal. These methods are often limited when dealing with low signal-to-noise ratio, mixed interference, or highly dynamic signal environments. By combining time-frequency analysis with deep learning, interference recognition can be formulated as a data-driven pattern classification problem, allowing automatic extraction of discriminative features from spectrogram-like representations.

2. Main Task

This project aims to investigate intelligent recognition of communication/navigation interference signals using time-frequency analysis and deep learning techniques. The student will first model or simulate several representative interference types, such as single-tone interference, multi-tone interference, narrowband interference, broadband noise interference, chirp interference, pulsed interference, and sweep interference. A dataset containing around 5,000–15,000 signal samples under different SNR or JSR conditions is recommended.

The student will then generate time-frequency representations using methods such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), wavelet transform, or other suitable approaches, and compare their effectiveness. Based on these representations, a classifier using CNN, ResNet, MobileNet, Vision Transformer, or a hybrid deep network will be designed and trained. The project should compare multiple architectures and evaluate robustness under different noise levels, especially under low-SNR conditions.

Quantitative research targets may include classification accuracy of above 90% under moderate conditions and above 80% under low-SNR scenarios, together with clear confusion matrix analysis and robustness evaluation.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a simulated interference dataset, a complete time-frequency feature extraction and classification pipeline, and a trained deep learning model for interference recognition. The final report should demonstrate the ability of the proposed method to distinguish multiple interference categories with satisfactory robustness. Evaluation should include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, and sensitivity to SNR/JSR variations. This topic is well aligned with the strengths of electronic information engineering, intelligent signal processing, and communication systems, and is particularly suitable for students considering postgraduate study in communications, signal processing, or navigation.
