1. Background

Roads and bridges are key components of modern transportation infrastructure, and their service safety is closely related to regular inspection and maintenance. Surface defects such as cracks, potholes, spalling, exposed reinforcement, and water seepage may gradually develop into serious structural problems if not identified at an early stage. Conventional manual inspection methods are often labor-intensive, subjective, slow, and difficult to scale, especially in large-area or hard-to-access scenarios. With recent advances in deep learning and computer vision, image-based automatic defect detection has become a highly promising approach for intelligent infrastructure inspection.

For Hainan and similar coastal or rapidly developing regions, the need for efficient transportation maintenance and digital infrastructure management is increasing. Therefore, a practical and lightweight AI-based detection system is of clear engineering relevance. Since deployment on mobile or edge devices is desirable in real applications, both detection accuracy and computational efficiency should be considered.

2. Main Task

This project aims to develop a lightweight deep learning framework for automatic detection and quantitative assessment of road and bridge surface defects. The student will first review common defect categories and prepare a labeled dataset using public data and/or self-collected images. A dataset of approximately 1,500–3,000 images covering at least 4–6 common defect typesis recommended. The project will then implement a baseline model using architectures such as YOLOv8, YOLOv10, RT-DETR, or lightweight segmentation networks, followed by optimization for small-target detection, robustness under illumination variation, and reduced model complexity.

Possible technical improvements include data augmentation, attention mechanisms, lightweight backbones, pruning, and feature fusion strategies. In addition to defect localization, the student is encouraged to explore basic quantitative indicators such as crack length, defect area, or severity level estimation. The target is to achieve mAP@0.5 above 80% , with an inference speed suitable for near real-time testing, e.g., above 15–20 FPS on a standard GPU platform.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a defect image dataset, a trained lightweight detection model, a comparative evaluation against baseline methods, and a prototype interface for result visualization. The final system should be able to identify major surface defects and provide basic quantitative inspection outputs. The dissertation is expected to include model design, experimental validation, ablation studies, and performance comparison in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, mAP, inference speed, and model size. This project is suitable for students interested in AI, computer vision, and intelligent infrastructure applications.

Background:

Because UAV images are usually captured from high altitude and oblique viewpoints, the objects in the images are often small, densely distributed, partially occluded, and mixed with complex backgrounds. In this project, object detection clearly means recognizing and locating targets captured in UAV aerial images, such as vehicles, pedestrians, and other ground objects, rather than detecting the UAV itself. Traditional supervised methods usually rely on labeled data and task-specific model training, while large language models provide new possibilities for relation extraction through instruction following, prompt design, in-context learning, and stronger semantic understanding. Main tasks:

1. Background


Network traffic measurement plays a fundamental role in modern network

management by providing essential traffic state information for tasks

such as anomaly detection, load balancing, and quality-of-service

assurance. However, due to the severely constrained memory and

computational resources of commodity switches, achieving fine-grained

and accurate traffic measurement at scale remains a significant

challenge. To improve measurement efficiency under resource constraints,

network-level collaborative measurement has emerged as a promising

approach. Rather than measuring all traffic independently at each

switch, measurement tasks are distributed across multiple switch nodes

in a coordinated manner, avoiding redundant monitoring of the same

flow and enabling each switch to focus on a distinct subset of

passing traffic. This collaborative paradigm improves both resource

utilization and measurement accuracy across the network. Nevertheless, the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of real-world

network traffic makes static task allocation strategies inadequate.

The measurement workload varies continuously across switches, and

suboptimal allocation decisions can lead to coverage gaps or resource

waste. This project addresses the dynamic allocation of collaborative

measurement tasks through a multi-agent reinforcement learning

framework, in which distributed switch agents learn to coordinate

their measurement strategies adaptively in response to evolving

traffic conditions, without requiring centralized control or

prior knowledge of traffic distributions.





2. Main task




（1）Study the fundamental principles of data center networks;




（2）Master widely used traffic measurement methods in data center networks;




（3）Learn typical reinforcement learning methods;




（4）Design a cooperative traffic measurement method based on muti-agent reinforcement learning algorithms;




（5）Perform simulation validation and continuous improvement of the proposed algorithm;




（6）Complete the undergraduate thesis.






3. Expected outcomes




(1) An intelligent system for cooperative network traffic measurement;




(2) An undergraduate thesis based on the research and implementation of the above system.

rows.themeProjectDescription: The concentration and particle size distribution of suspended particles in solution are important parameters for assessing water quality, pharmaceutical purity, and the quality of chemical liquids. This project aims to develop a rapid detection method based on the principle of light scattering. When a light beam passes through a solution containing particles, scattered light is generated at specific angles. The intensity of the scattered light is proportional to the particle concentration, while the angular distribution of the scattered light is related to the particle size. This research plans to design a miniature optical path system, using a laser light source and high-sensitivity photodetectors, to construct a portable detection device. By measuring the scattered light intensity and angular distribution, combined with inversion calculations based on the Mie scattering model, the project aims to achieve simultaneous quantitative analysis of particle concentration and size. This method requires no complex pretreatment, offers rapid response, and is non-contact and non-destructive. It is expected to provide an efficient, online tool for particle detection in environmental monitoring, the pharmaceutical industry, and process control.

This project aims to develop a high-precision, rapid fabrication method for polymer optical waveguides by combining digital light processing (DLP) technology with a light-induced self-writing polymer process. Utilizing the high-resolution dynamic masking capability of DLP technology, a pre-designed patterned light beam is projected into a photosensitive polymer precursor solution. Localized photopolymerization is initiated by the light, enabling one-step self-writing formation of the waveguide structure, thereby avoiding the complex mask fabrication and development steps inherent in traditional photolithography. The study will systematically investigate the effects of exposure dosage, light intensity distribution, and polymer formulation on the waveguide geometry and optical performance, and will characterize key parameters such as propagation loss and mode coupling. This work aims to establish a flexible and efficient new strategy for polymer optical waveguide manufacturing, providing technical support for the development of on-chip optical interconnects, optical sensing, and flexible photonic devices.

Background:

Forest fires are important ecological and environmental disturbances that can cause vegetation loss, biodiversity degradation, soil erosion, carbon emissions, and threats to human life and property. Sichuan Province has complex topography, diverse climate conditions, rich forest resources, and significant spatial differences in vegetation types and human activities. These factors make forest fire occurrence highly heterogeneous in both space and time. In recent years, climate variability, extreme weather events, land use change, and increasing human activities have further influenced forest fire risk. Understanding the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of forest fires in Sichuan Province is therefore important for fire prevention, ecological protection, disaster risk management, and sustainable forest resource planning. Attribution analysis can help identify the key driving factors behind fire occurrence and provide scientific support for regional forest fire monitoring and early warning.

Main Task:

The main task of this project is to analyze the spatiotemporal distribution patterns and possible driving factors of forest fires in Sichuan Province. The student will first conduct a literature review on forest fire monitoring, spatial-temporal pattern analysis, and fire attribution methods. Then, forest fire occurrence data will be collected and organized, which may include satellite fire point products, burned area datasets, meteorological data, vegetation indices, topographic data, land use data, and human activity indicators. Data preprocessing may include coordinate transformation, spatial matching, temporal aggregation, missing value processing, and construction of analysis units. Based on these datasets, the student will analyze the temporal variation of forest fires at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, and investigate spatial clustering, hotspot distribution, and regional differences. Furthermore, attribution analysis will be conducted to explore the influence of factors such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed, humidity, elevation, slope, vegetation coverage, land use type, population density, and distance to roads or settlements. Possible methods include correlation analysis, regression models, random forest, geographic detector, or spatial statistical methods.

Expected Outcome:

The expected outcome of this project includes a structured forest fire dataset for Sichuan Province, a set of spatiotemporal analysis results, attribution analysis of major driving factors, source code or GIS workflows, and visualized maps and charts. The student is expected to reveal the temporal trends, seasonal characteristics, spatial hotspots, and regional differences of forest fires in Sichuan Province. The project should identify the key natural and human-related factors associated with forest fire occurrence and explain their possible mechanisms. The final results may provide useful reference for forest fire prevention, risk zoning, ecological management, and disaster mitigation. Through this project, the student will gain practical experience in remote sensing data processing, GIS spatial analysis, environmental data integration, statistical modeling, and scientific thesis writing.
rows.themeTitle: Spatiotemporal Evolution Characteristics and Attribution Analysis of Forest Fires in Sichuan Province

As social and humanoid robots become increasingly integrated into healthcare, education, customer service, and assistive living environments, the ability to communicate naturally and effectively with humans is becoming a critical requirement. Future robots must not only perceive speech and visual cues but also understand emotions, adapt to multilingual users, and engage in empathetic and context-aware conversations.


This project theme focuses on developing intelligent perception, communication, and interaction capabilities for social robots using artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, speech processing, natural language processing, and affective computing. Students will design and implement key components that enable robots to perceive human emotions, understand spoken language, and generate appropriate responses to improve the quality of human–robot interaction.


The projects are centred around the development and integration of AI-driven modules that can ultimately contribute to a multimodal emotionally intelligent robotic assistant capable of interacting naturally with users in real-world scenarios.


Project Title 1: Speech-Based Emotion Recognition for Social Robots

This project focuses on developing an audio-only emotion recognition system that enables robots to understand human emotional states through speech signals. It leverages machine learning to extract and classify emotional cues from spoken language, helping robots respond empathetically in real-time.


Project Title 2: Facial Emotion Recognition for Social Robots

This project aims to build a computer vision-based system that allows a robot to recognize human emotions by analysing facial expressions. Using images or video input and deep learning techniques, the robot will infer emotions visually in real-time, enhancing multimodal HRI.


Project Title 3: Multilingual Language Identification for Emotion-Aware Human-Robot Interaction

As social robots are increasingly deployed in multilingual environments, they must be able to identify the language being spoken before applying language-specific processing. This project aims to develop a real-time Language Identification (LID) system using speech processing and AI techniques, providing a foundation for future multilingual emotion recognition and conversational human–robot interaction systems.


Project Title 4: Empathetic Conversational AI for Emotion-Aware Human-Robot Interaction

Effective human–robot interaction requires robots to respond appropriately not only to what users say but also to how they feel. This project aims to develop an empathetic conversational AI system that generates emotionally appropriate responses based on the user's detected emotional state, conversational context, and interaction history. This project aims to explore large language models, dialogue management systems, emotion-aware response generation, and conversational design techniques to create more engaging and supportive robot interactions.

Non-contact speech recognition based on inductive effects investigates whether weak electromagnetic variations generated during acoustic playback or vibration can be captured and processed to recover speech-related information. Speakers, earphones and similar acoustic devices are widely used in online meetings, voice calls and smart terminals. Prior open-domain research on magnetic side channels, such as MagEar, shows that a speaker does not only produce audible sound; its electromagnetic structure may also radiate weak time-varying magnetic signals. These signals are difficult to use directly because they are extremely weak, strongly affected by distance, orientation and environmental interference, and different from normal microphone recordings. This project therefore focuses on a controlled, consent-based laboratory prototype for privacy-aware acoustic sensing and defensive evaluation. The main task of this project is to design and evaluate a lightweight non-contact speech acquisition and recognition system using an inductive sensing chain, an ESP32-S3 based acquisition platform, local backend processing, Web-based control and speech enhancement or recognition algorithms. Specifically, this project includes the following tasks:

Survey existing studies on magnetic side-channel sensing, inductive weak-signal acquisition, non-acoustic speech recovery, speech enhancement and automatic speech recognition. Then summarise why inductive speech sensing is challenging, including weak signal strength, fast distance attenuation, circuit noise, environmental electromagnetic interference and audio distortion.

Develop a prototype non-contact speech recognition framework based on inductive sensing. The project may include an inductor sensing front end, analogue signal conditioning, I2S audio sampling, ESP32-S3 wireless streaming, a Node.js backend, a Web control interface, raw and enhanced audio file management, denoising, and optional speech-to-text processing.

Evaluate the proposed prototype under different system settings and controlled scenarios. The main performance metrics may include signal-to-noise ratio, recovered audio intelligibility, MFCC cosine similarity, MOSNet or subjective listening score, automatic speech recognition accuracy, word error rate, recording stability, system latency, robustness to distance, angle, device type and environmental interference, and implementation complexity.

The neck network of the model was optimized by integrating the bidirectional feature path enhancement concept from the Hierarchical Scale Feature Pyramid Network (HS-FPN) and the Path Aggregation Network (PAN), thereby achieving Hierarchical Scale Feature Fusion (HS-PAN). Smartphone camera fingerprint recognition is an important technique in multimedia forensics and civilian device authenticity verification. Existing camera fingerprint methods usually extract sensor noise residuals, PRNU, noiseprint features, or other imaging-pipeline traces from still images. However, a single still image may provide limited fingerprint evidence because it can be affected by scene content, lighting conditions, compression, and post-processing. A live photo or motion photo contains not only a still image, but also a short sequence of video frames, and may include timing information and an optional audio track. These additional signals may provide richer evidence for smartphone source verification. The main task of this project is to investigate whether live or motion photo frames can improve camera fingerprint recognition compared with ordinary still images. The project is based on open research literature and consent-based laboratory data collection, and is designed for civilian applications only. It does not involve person identification, user tracking, or surveillance applications. Specifically, this project includes the following tasks:


Survey existing studies on source camera identification, PRNU, noiseprint, smartphone video forensics, and live/motion photo formats. Then summarise why continuous video frames and frame-level traces may provide stronger camera fingerprint evidence than a single still image.

Develop a simple live/motion photo processing framework. The framework should extract the key still image, video frames, frame timing information, and optional audio track if available. It should then implement or reproduce a representative camera fingerprint method, such as Noiseprint or PRNU-based residual analysis, and extend it from still images to multiple video frames.

Evaluate the proposed framework on a small consent-based smartphone dataset and compare it with a still-image baseline. The main performance metrics may include device identification accuracy, true-model pass rate, wrong-model rejection rate, false accept rate, false reject rate, disturbance rate, balanced accuracy, equal error rate, coverage, and implementation complexity.

1.Background

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) represent an emerging paradigm that combines physical constraints with data-driven methodologies. By incorporating physical laws to guide the learning process, PINNs enhance model generalization, especially in data-scarce or high-noise environments. During training, PINNs embed physical principles directly into the learning algorithm. Consequently, the neural network is not only adjusted to fit the observed data but is also governed by physical laws, ensuring that the learned solutions both conform to the data and adhere to physical consistency. This approach substantially improves simulation speed and accuracy while preserving result interpretability, thereby offering an efficient and reliable new pathway for the simulation of physical fields in power equipment.

1.Background

Transformers operating under complex conditions are subjected to thermal, mechanical, and electrical stresses, which inevitably result in various types of short-circuit faults. Under such fault conditions, leakage magnetic flux within the transformer and the resulting electromagnetic forces acting on the windings can cause winding deformation, accelerating equipment degradation and compromising operational performance and service life. To enable real-time and high-precision condition monitoring of transformers across different operating scenarios, the correlation between electrical parameters and operational states can be leveraged to predict internal magnetic flux distribution, thereby facilitating the analysis and diagnosis of internal condition integrity. Consequently, investigating the real-time variation of electromagnetic parameters and internal magnetic flux in transformers is of great significance for ensuring the stability of transformer operation.

2.Main task

The student should understand the state-of-the-art in magnetic flux prediction for three-phase transformer windings under short-circuit fault conditions.

The student should compare various machine learning-based approaches for magnetic flux prediction in three-phase transformer windings under short-circuit fault conditions and identify the optimal algorithm.

3.Expected outcomes

The student should find a high-precision algorithm for predicting magnetic flux in three-phase transformer windings under short-circuit fault conditions.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1 Background

State Space Models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, offering linear computational complexity in long-sequence modeling while maintaining competitive performance. However, the growing parameter sizes of SSMs create significant deployment challenges on resource-constrained edge devices. Model compression techniques—structured pruning, quantization, and low-rank decomposition—are essential for lightweight deployment, but they introduce complex trade-offs among compression ratio, inference speed, accuracy retention, and hardware energy efficiency. Traditional single-objective compression approaches fail to capture these competing demands. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) such as NSGA-II and MOEA/D provide a principled framework for navigating these trade-offs by generating Pareto-optimal solution sets. Furthermore, assessing compression strategies solely on GPU metrics overlooks the energy efficiency characteristics of emerging compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators, which are critical for embodied AI applications. CIM-MLC (architecture-level) and NeuroSim (circuit-level) are two complementary simulation tools for CIM energy estimation.

2 Main Task

This project develops an automated multi-objective compression framework for SSMs that jointly optimizes four objectives:

(i) model compression ratio,

(ii) inference throughput,

(iii) accuracy retention on downstream tasks, and

(iv) energy efficiency on CIM simulators.

The student will first survey SSM architectures (Mamba, Mamba2) and compression methodologies. Then, a modular compression pipeline will be implemented, supporting structured pruning, INT8/FP16 quantization, and low-rank factorization. NSGA-II and MOEA/D will be integrated to search the high-dimensional configuration space, with Pareto front convergence analysis across algorithms. Critically, compressed models will be evaluated not only on standard benchmarks (e.g., long-range arena) but also on CIM simulators to quantify actual energy-performance trade-offs. The primary evaluation tool is CIM-MLC; NeuroSim can be used as an alternative circuit-level estimator.

Tasks

• Survey SSM architecture fundamentals (Mamba, Mamba2) and existing model compression techniques

• Formulate SSM compression as a multi-objective optimization problem (compression ratio vs. accuracy vs. speed vs. energy)

• Implement a compression evaluation pipeline supporting pruning, quantization, and low-rank decomposition

• Apply NSGA-II and MOEA/D to search optimal compression configurations and compare their Pareto fronts

• Evaluate compressed SSM models on long-sequence benchmarks and CIM simulators (CIM-MLC primary, NeuroSim alternative) for energy-performance trade-offs

• Compare SSM compression Pareto fronts against Transformer compression to analyze architectural advantages

3 Expected Outcomes

The project will deliver:

(a) a comparative analysis of Pareto fronts achieved by different MOEAs for SSM compression;

(b) an open-source compression-evaluation toolkit integrating CIM-MLC (with NeuroSim as alternative) for energy modeling;

(c) empirical guidelines for selecting compression strategies based on deployment constraints; and

(d) validation that multi-objective optimization outperforms single-objective baselines in balancing accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

Results may contribute to a conference submission or technical report.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Multi-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems are required to perform full-coverage scanning over extensive target areas for missions such as border patrol, post-disaster area assessment and large-scale farm monitoring. In practical operations, UAVs are subject to multiple constraints, including limited communication bandwidth caused by signal attenuation and interference, restricted communication range that may lead to disconnection beyond effective coverage, as well as battery capacity limitations characterized by short endurance and mandatory return for recharging. Traditional coverage planning methods generally assume ideal communication conditions and unlimited energy supply, which often results in communication outages or power depletion during actual flight. It remains a challenging task to achieve complete area coverage via cooperative planning of multiple UAVs under dual constraints of communication and energy, while minimizing total energy consumption and flight duration. This project investigates cooperative coverage planning strategies for multi-UAV systems with communication and energy limitations, aiming to enhance the robustness and practicality of the overall system. The main research tasks are specified as follows:

1) Constraint Modeling and Problem Formalization

Establish UAV communication range models, signal attenuation models (e.g., free-space path loss model) and energy consumption models correlated with flight speed, travel distance and payload. Formulate communication connectivity constraints requiring each UAV to maintain connection with at least one in-range UAV, and energy feasibility constraints stipulating that the total energy consumption of flight paths shall not exceed battery capacity. The cooperative coverage planning problem is ultimately formalized as a constrained combinatorial optimization problem.

2) Area Decomposition and Coverage PathGeneration

Propose an area decomposition approach based on grid graphs or Voronoi diagrams to partition the large target region into multiple subregions and assign each subregion to individual UAVs. For each divided subregion, generate global coverage paths adopting Boustrophedon scanning or spiral coverage patterns. The number of turns is further optimized to reduce overall energy consumption.

3) Communication Relay and Energy Coordination Strategy

Develop an inter-UAV communication relay mechanism. When a UAV suffers weak signals due to excessive distance from the base station, another UAV will be dynamically scheduled as a relay node to sustain the connectivity of the entire UAV swarm. Meanwhile, an energy-balanced task scheduling scheme is designed to assign more coverage tasks to UAVs with sufficient remaining power, so as to prevent early return of individual UAVs.

4) Simulation Validation and Performance Evaluation

Construct a large-scale outdoor simulation environment with undulating terrain sized at 500 m × 500 m using Gazebo or AirSim, where 3 to 5 quadrotor UAVs are deployed. Comparative experiments are conducted against classic coverage planning without constraint consideration, schemes with only energy constraints and schemes with only communication constraints. Evaluation metrics include full coverage rate, maximum variance of energy consumption, number of communication interruptions and total mission time. A visualization interface is also developed to display real-time communication link status and residual energy during cooperative coverage operations.
rows.themeTitle: Research on collaborative coverage planning for multi-UAV systems under communication and energy constraints

Electric energy serves as a vital energy source in daily life. By 2024, China's per capita annual residential electricity consumption had approached 1,000 kWh, highlighting the essential role of electricity in people's daily routines. Transmission lines, as key infrastructure for power transportation, maintain stability that is directly tied to the reliability of electricity supply. In China, the humid and cold winters in the southern region, along with the severe cold in the central and northern regions, frequently result in ice coating disasters on transmission lines. Moreover, global warming and the increasing frequency of extreme weather events pose significant threats to the safety of transmission lines. Conventional manual inspection methods are inefficient and fail to satisfy the demands of real-time monitoring. Recent substantial advancements in deep learning within computer vision—especially breakthroughs in semantic segmentation algorithms for image recognition—offer novel solutions for detecting ice coating on transmission lines. rows.themeProjectDescription:
After the occurrence of natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods and wildfires, cooperative search and rescue (SAR) with multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can rapidly cover large-scale complex terrains and improve the efficiency of survivor detection. Nevertheless, the SAR environment presents

multiple challenges, including uneven distribution of mission points, limited endurance of UAVs, dynamically changing communication topologies, and time-decaying mission values. These characteristics render traditional task allocation methods incapable of real-time adaptation to dynamic scenarios. Moreover, such methods lack the capability to structurally model the complex interactions among agents, thus failing to achieve real-time and efficient task allocation. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can effectively represent the heterogeneous relational graph between UAVs and missions, and learn optimal allocation strategies by exploiting topological information. Accordingly, this project leverages the representation learning capability of GNNs for non-Euclidean data to investigate multi-UAV task allocation methods tailored for SAR scenarios, aiming to maximize overall search-and-rescue benefits and minimize mission completion time. The main research contents are outlined as follows:

1) SAR Scenario Modeling and Graph Construction

Formulate the multi-UAV SAR task allocation problem in a formal manner. UAVs and mission points are defined as two types of nodes in a heterogeneous graph. Edge features incorporate the distance from UAVs to mission points, mission priority, time window constraints and communication topological relationships.

A dynamic task allocation model is established based on Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (Dec-POMDP).

2) Design of GNN-based Allocation Strategy

Develop a task allocation decision module based on Graph Attention Networks (GAT) or Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN). Features of neighboring UAVs and missions are aggregated via message passing to output the allocation probability or marginal benefit of each UAV for individual missions. The Hungarian algorithm or greedy matching is adopted to convert probability outputs into feasible task allocation schemes.

3) Online Reallocation Mechanism for Dynamic Environments

To address dynamic events during SAR operations, including newly detected missions, UAV malfunctions and return-to-base for recharging, an incremental GNN-based task reallocation approach is proposed. By exploiting the locality of graph topology, only the embeddings of affected nodes are updated, so as to realize

low-latency online re-planning.

4) Simulation Verification and Performance Comparison

Construct SAR simulation environments based on AirSim or ROS combined with Gazebo, which cover terrains with obstacles, 10 to 20 mission points and 3 to 5 UAVs. Comparative experiments are conducted against classic greedy allocation, the Hungarian algorithm and reinforcement learning-based allocation methods. The

performance of the proposed method is evaluated in terms of mission completion rate, total flight distance and reallocation response time. Meanwhile, a visualization interface is developed to dynamically display the allocation graph and UAV flight paths during the whole process.
rows.themeTitle: Graph neural network based task allocation method for multi-UAV search and rescue missions

rows.themeProjectDescription:
With the development of bionic robots, human-robot interaction, teleoperation, and intelligent prosthetic hands, five-finger dexterous hands have attracted increasing attention due to their human-like grasping and manipulation capabilities. Traditional control methods for dexterous hands mainly rely on buttons, manual teaching, or predefined motion patterns, making it difficult to achieve natural and intuitive human-machine interaction. Gesture recognition technology can capture the operator’s hand motion intention, while motion mapping can convert human hand movements into joint motions of the dexterous hand, thereby improving the flexibility and interactivity of dexterous hand control. Therefore, this project focuses on the bionic control requirements of five-finger dexterous hands and investigates a dexterous hand control method based on gesture recognition and motion mapping, aiming to realize the conversion and control from human hand motions to dexterous hand motions. The main research contents are as follows:

1) Study the mechanical structure, actuation mechanism, and basic grasping motions of the five-finger dexterous hand, and analyze the functional requirements and overall scheme of the dexterous hand control system.

2) Investigate gesture acquisition and recognition methods. Use cameras, data gloves, or sensors to collect human hand motion information, and realize the recognition of typical gestures such as hand opening, fist clenching, pinching, and pointing.

3) Analyze the correspondence between human hand joint motions and dexterous hand joint motions. Design a motion mapping method from human gestures to dexterous hand movements to achieve multiple grasping postures of the dexterous hand.

4) Build a five-finger dexterous hand control experimental platform or simulation platform. Test the gesture recognition accuracy, motion response speed, and execution performance of the dexterous hand, and verify the feasibility and effectiveness of the designed system.
rows.themeTitle: Design of a Five-Finger Dexterous Hand Control System Based on Gesture Recognition and Motion Mapping

rows.themeProjectDescription: Most time series are globally non-stationary, but they exhibit good stationarity within local intervals, allowing for fitting with suitable functions. The research object of this project is the measured values of time series collected by industrial sensors. The main goal of the research is to segment long time series into short slices to obtain the best fit. Firstly, statistical analysis is conducted on the variation characteristics of the time series to identify inflection points and divide the curve into multiple local segments, each maintaining a good variation trend and statistical characteristics. Next, a set of fitting curve functions is constructed. Finally, based on machine learning methods, each segment is classified to generate the optimal fitting function for the segment, achieving smaller errors.
